- A BIRD'S SUMMER SONG. The bird sang in the early spring, When trees and flowers were blossoming, "Oh, summer days are coming I" , , He sang it all through blooming May, And the woothdoves answered day by day, And the golden bees were humming. The nest was built, the eggs were there, The birdlings all were hatched with care, And soon away were flying. What cared they now for sheltering nest? V. • - 'The world was theirs for summer quest, The world in beauty lying. Yet though his nestlings all had flown, - Upon the elder-bough alone, The summer bird sat singing; • Through hot July with lilies crowned, • His voice still filled the woods around, Joy to the listeners bringing. —Mini" Little Folk?' Maya:ine for August.

WREN JACK IS TALL AND TWENTY. ' When Jack is tall and twenty, We know what Jack will do; - With girls so sweet and plenty, He'll find him one to woo. And soon the lovers' twilight Will hear a story told, And Jack will die or fly sky-high For sake of hair of gold. Hearken, Jack, and heed me— Ponder what I say! fools are sold for locks of gold, For gold will turn to grey. But Jack, if truth be spoken, Is simple Jack no more; If gold his heart has broken, 'Tis scarce the gold of yore. He wots of dower for daughters Not all in ringlets roll'd; To beauty steerd, his heart will yield: To stamped and minted gold. 11 Hearken, Jack, and heed me— Ponder what I say! If gold hath wing, as poets sing, Then gold may fleet away. When Jack goes forth a-wooing, If Jack has heart or head, And would not soon be rueing The hour that saw him wed, He will not pine for graces, Nor cringe for wealth to hold, But strive and dare by service fair To win a heart of gold. Hearken, Jack, and heed me— Ponder what I say! The gear will fly, the bloom will die, But love will last for aye. FREDERICK LANOBRIDGE.
—Good Words.

Enjoy the blessings of this day, if God sencls them, and the evils bear patiently and sweetly, for this day only is ours; we are dead to yesterday and are not born to-mor- row. As it is with our physical health so it is with our men- tal troubles, that which ails us for the moment seems, While it lasts, to be the most serious calamity that can befall us. "I never give to beggars in the street," remarked a young man to a beggar.' "Will yer honour oblige me with your name and address and I'll call on you,' was the prompt retort. God is attracting our regard in and through all things. Every flower is a hint of His beauty; every grain of wheat is a token of his benevolence; every atom of dust is a revelation of his power. "Have you," asked the Judge of a recently convicted Juan, "anything to offer the Court before sentence is passed 2" No, your honour," replied the prisoner ; "my lawyer took my last farthing." There is no profession so forbidding, no work so crabbed, that a man who strives to extract the utmost happiness from it may not twine about it roses of fancy and hide the most of its thorns. If you have a duty to do, do it straightforwardly. An .old army commander was accustomed to say, as he saw a younger officer dodge his head at the whistle of a bullet, You foolish fellow, you'll dodge right in the way of a bullet !" A little girl, aged nine, called her father to her bed- side the other evening. "Papa," said the little diplomat," I want to ask your advice." "Well, my dear, what as it about?" "What do you think it will be best to give me on my birthday ?" The Irishman explained that he was smiling because he had seen his cousin from Cork that day. On being I asked if there was good news from home, he replied, "I only saw him across the street; and when I ran up to him, I found he was not the man:' THE CENTRE OF ALL RELIGIONS.—To love God with all our heart and soul and mind, and our neighbour as ourselves, is salvation. If that end can be reached by any human being, in any method, whether as a Jew or a Greek, whether as a Christian, or Buddhist, or Brahmin, that man is saved—for he has become that which God wishes him to be.—Dr. Donald Macleod, in "Good • Words" for August. Dry Goods Merchant: "So, sir, you think you could learn to become a salesman?" "Yes, sir." "Well, sup- pose you were waiting on that man and his wife over there at the lace counter. What would you do first?" "I should hold up the best piece of lace in the stock and ask the man if he didn't think it becoming to his daugh- ter's style of beauty." Well, what then ?" "Oh, nothing; the woman would take care of the rest of it." "Young man, I don't want you for a clerk. I want you for a partner." Balzac being asked to explain an abstruse ssage in one of his books frankly owned that it had no meaning at all. " You see," said he, "for the average reader all that is clear seems easy, and if I did not sometimes give him a complicated and meaningless sentence, he would think he knew as much as myself. But when he comes upon something that he cannot comprehend he rereads it, puzzles over it, takes his head between his hands, and glares at it, and finding it impossible to make head or tail of it, says, "Great man, tßalzac, he knows more' than I do !" Pintstaw DELICACIES. While speaking of butchers' sheps I ought not to omit to refer to those specially devoted to the sale of horse and ass flesh. They are kept in the same cleanly way as those which confine themselves to the ordinary meat. A very curious sight for a foreigner, both at the i markets and n the barrows is the edible snail. It is of a pale gray or a light brown colour, the choicest varieties coming from the wine dis- tricts. I saw a barro i stful one day n Rue Mouffetard. They were very fat and lively, and those which were out of the shell were as large as a labourer's finger. :-The coster was selling them at 25 centimes each.--Good

Words. James Henderson had served his country sb long in the saddle that his knees had become quite stiff, and, • consequently, lame. He was retired with a pension shortly after Waterloo, and returned to Leslie, his native place. Each receipt of his pension was made the occa- sion of a grand spree on Jamie's part. He was found on one of these occasions, early in the morning, lying help- less its the gutter, near his house, by the young daughter of a neighbour. Helping Jamie to rise, she said to him, " Why, Jamie, what's the matter ? " "Eh, Jeanie, this is the effects o' Waterloo! Ye see I canna lift my feet free the stanes like ither folk. Eh, lassie to think that 1, who lived through Waterloo, should die at last in a -Leslie gutter!" A CURIOUS HOJIAGE.—At Chingford, in Epping Forest, there was, some hundreds of years ago, an estate called Brindwoods, which had originally belonged to the rector of the parish, and had been given to another person 'on Condition that he and his successors did homage to the rector. Every time the property changed owners, the new proprietor, with his wife, man-servant, and maid- servant, each riding on horseback, had to go to the rectory. The master took a horn with him, and carried a hawk on his fist, while the man-servant had a grey- hound, to the use of both of which the rector was en- titled all that day if he desired to go hawking. On arrival at the parsonage, the gentleman blew three blasts on his horn to let the rector know of his arrival. The rector then gave him a chicken for the hawk, a peck of oats for the horse, and a loaf for the grey-hound. All then dined 'together, and when the master started home he again blew three blasts on his horn. This quaint ceremony has, however, long been in disuse.-.Litt e Follcs for August. ARE STAYS NECESSARY?—Many women assert that they derive great comfort from stays, that they support the body admirably, and without them the wearer feels in- clined to " drop to pieces." All this may b:4 perfectly true. But what significance must we attach to the state- ment that certain women cannot possibly do without stays? Do they mean for one moment to assert that the human body is so ill-constructed and so badly adapted fo; its purpose in life that it has to depend for its integrity upon the productions of a corset maker? Such an assumption is simply outrageous, the true explana- tion being that by the persistent use of stays the muscles of the back have become so enfeebled (from prolonged disuse) that they are no longer able to support the spine. " Those who declare, therefore, that they cannot do with- out stays, adopt the argument of the opium-eater, who rusintaijis that he cannot do without his opium. The long-continued use of the drug has so impaired his sys- tem that he feels a constant cravin," for it. And those who cannot exist unless braced uply corsets have so enfeebled a part of their system that they cannot do without the support upon which they have so long de- pended.—The Book of Health. ....-687ABLISHRD NEARLY 50 YEARS. div.head: HOLKER HERD.
div.p: THE HOLKER HERD.

A correspondeiit—se-Js-U-s—die-falOWing addtional par- ticulars respecting the Holker herd of shorthorn cattle, the property of the Duke of Devonshire : • A sale of cattle was held at Holker previous to 1851, at which an average of 22 guineas was realised, but there is no individual record of it. On September 12, 1851, Mr. Strafford, of London, sold the entire herd, compris- ing 56 head, which realised a total of £1,407, an average of £25 2s. 6d. A fresh start was then made, and Mr. Strafford held his next sale on Friday, September 9th, 1864. In 1853, Mr. Drewry had purchased Oxford 15th, at Tortworth, for 200 guineas; and in 1867, he bought Lady Oxford sth, at Havering Park, for 600 guineas. From these two cows all' the Holker Oxfords have descended. At this 1864 sale, six of the animals realised upwards of 100 guineas each—three bulls and three cows,—namely, 210g5., 155g5., 105g5., 155g5., 135g5., and 130g5., big prices in these days. 19 cows averaged £64 4s. 4d.; 11 bulls averaged £69 9s. 10d. The 30 head sold for £1,984 10s., or a general average of £66 3s. In Sep- tember, 1871, Mr. Strafford was again at Holker, and sold 31 cows and heifers for an average of £248 2s. Od. ; 12 bulls averaged £221 us.; 43 head averaged £240 13s. 10d., or a total of £10,349 17s. In September of 1874, Mr. Strafford offered 28 cows and heifers, which averaged £462 Bs. 3d.; 15 bulls averaged £236 13s. lid. The 43 head averaged £383 13s. 30., or a total of £16,497 12s. This was the highest average of any draft sale up to that time ; but it was to be eclipsed by the next sale, which took place at Holker on September 18th, 18'18, Mr. Straf- ford's last appearance there. Then 18 cows and heifers averaged £794 us. 2d.; 12 bulls averaged £468 7s. 9d. The 30 head averaged £664 is. 10d., or a total of £19,922 14s. At this sale seven of the animals made over 1,000 guineas each, the highest being 2,660 guineas. A PHILANTHROPIC MERCHANT.—An account of Jonas Hanway, who lies in the old graveyard at Hanwell, will ,be found in Dr. Smiles's "Self-Help." The sbn of a ; storekeeper in the dockyard at Portsmouth, he was ierought up to a mercantile career, and made a fortune by trading in Russia. That fortune he spent in works of public utility and benevolence. He improved the high- ways of the metropolis; he organised a volunteer body lof marines;' he founded the Marine Society (which is kill one of the largest and most important of London I charities); he largely re-modelled, the Foundling Hos- pital.; he was. one of the founders of the Magdalen; like Howard, he explored the fever dens of the poorer classes of London, and forced on the parochial asithorities a. system of registration; in order to protect infant life; he got an Act passed for the protection of climbing boys employed by chimney-sweeps; and, strange to say, was rewarded by. the Government for his philanthropic efforts by being made a member of the Victualling Board. "His moral courage," writes Dr. Smiles, "was of the first order. It may be regarded as a trivial matter to men- tion that he was the first who ventured to walk the I streets of London with an umbrella over his head. But i let any modern London merchant venture to walk alongl Cornhill with a peaked Chinese hat and he will find that , it takes some moral courage to persevere in it. After carrying an umbrella for some thirty years, Mr. Hanway saw the article at length come into general use." Jonas Hanway died childless, and he left his fortune to those whom he had befriended in his lifetime.—" Cassells Greater London." A REMINISCENCE OF THE PRESS-GANG DAYS.—And again., Mother, about to visit her family in South Wales, has taken her passage in a sailing vessel from Falmouth to Swansea. She is arranging her multifarious luggage on board, when a handsome young sailor, of a singularly agreeable appearance, rushes into her cabin. The press- gams is coming, he says, "and is sure to seize him, the only young and likely man on board. He has just re- turned from a lone voyage. Will the lady save him from this cruel fate'? Will she let him secrete himself among her luggage ?" Mother abhors the tyrannical custom of seizing men by force for service on Use ships of war, and full of compassion, consents to his conceal- ment. The king's officer with his men search the vessel. He next opens the door of mother's cabin, and appar- ently much out of humour, advances, cutlass in hand. Mother, looking up from her book or work, begs him to respect the privacy of her cabin. The captain of the press-gang makes a sign to his men to stand hack; but says, "He is bound to do his duty; a man is missing, whom he has reason to sup- pose is on board, therefore—" Mother, outwardly calm but inwardly terribly alarmed, interrupts him with the words, "I am a lady travelling alone, you are a gen- tleman." These words seem to disarm him. He offers a polite apology, and retiring, quits the vessel witltihis men. The moment they are gone thecaptain gives orders to sail. The rescued sailer creeps from his hiding-place, but is not allowed to show himself till they are out at sea. He becomes mother's devoted attendant during the long and stormy passage -which ensues; while she, the only female on board, receives extreme consideration from the captain and the entire crew, who regard her as a general benefaetress.—Mary Hewitt, in Good Words for August. THE CROFTERS LOVE FOR THE " AULD RAME."—The time came when kelp was driven from the market by the reduction of the duty on barilla„ and then the Mass of the people had to depend almost exclusively on their potato-crops, which even in good seasons were a very inadequate means of support. In bad seasons the wretched crofters and cotters had no resource but the charity of the landlords and the public. During the last thirty years the pressure has been in some degree re- lieved by emigration, and by the flow of a considerable part of the population to manufacturing towns; but there is still much chronic wretchedness in the crofting districts, nearly all of which are greatly over-crowded. ' Nor can the position of the crofters become really satis- factory until they are more evenly distributed over the country, and obtain larger and better holdings with the means of stocking them. Only then will they derive much solid advantage from security of tenure, fair rents, and compensation for improvements. The crofters are often censured for their unwillingness to emigrate, but those who blame them do not realise the strength of their attachment to their homes. A passionate love of their native hills and straths has always been a charac- teristic of the Scottish Highlanders— Glen Etive ! 0 Glen Etive ! There was raised my earliest home. Beautiful its woods at sunrise. When the sun struck on Glen Etive. Glendaruadh ! 0 Glendaruadh ! Each man who dwells there I love. Sweet the voice of the cuckoo on bending bough. On the hill above Glendaruadh. Beloved is Draighen and its sounding shore, Beloved the water over the clear pure sands. 0 that I might not depart from the east, Unless I go with my beloved.

These verses (quoted by Principal Shairp in his lecture on "The Poetry of the Scottish Highlands") are from a Gaelic poem which is found in a manuscript of the thirteenth century, and it expresses exactly the feeling of crofters who are driven by dire distress to seek their fortune in other lands. They love even the "black houses" in which they have been born and bred, wretched dwellings with poor little windows or with no , windows at all, and sheltering man and beast under the same roof.—The English Illustrated Magasine for August. We can hardly , realise that the scene was ever disturbed by the busy feet of martial men, and that the blast of the bugle once sounded in that wild waste. We regard the decay as typical of the country of its former rulers, whose power among nations has diminished to a very shadow. Within the city walls cultivated grounds and groves of bamboo fill much of the space, and some fine old timber ties planted by the Dutch and a few ruins yet remain to tell of its masters. Other parts within the walls pre- sent the features peculiar to a Chinese city, and certainly these are not attractive. Some little distance without the city is a great level plain, bleak and barren, but the spot le one of painful interest. It is known as the execution ground, and there, one August morning in 1842, about the close of the first Ang,lo-Chinese war, nearly two hundred shipwrecked per- sons were executed. There is no parallel to the story of the massacre. The terrible tragedy was enacted by order of the Chinese authorities. The Indian transport Ner- budda and the opium ship Ann were wrecked on the coast of Formosa, about forty Europeans escaping from the former to the mainland; the others were made pri- soners, and carried by their captors from the scene of the wreck to Tai-wan, where they were lodged in a Chinese prison. They were huddled together in a dis- gusting manner, male and female, and with I little or no clothing, anctraany died of hunger. The women suf- feeed the most frightful outrages, too horrid for recital, and gladly welcomed death. Excepting ten persons, the survivors of the double wreck were afterwards executed. They were heavily chained, and followed by an infuriated mob, such as only the slums of a Chinese city can pro- duce, the captives were driven to the execution ground, and being made to kneel, were one after another be- headed. One of the survivors, a Mr. Newman' gave the following account of the massacre and of his own singular deliverance :—" On being taken out of his sedan to have his hands shackled behind his back, he saw two of the prisoners with their irons off, and refusing to have them put on. He advised them to submit quietly, but they still refusing, he first wrenched off his own, and I then put them in theirs, to the great pleasure of the soldiers, but when the soldiers wished to replace his he declined. As they were on the point of securing him, he accidentally saw the chief officer seated close to him. Going before him, he threw himself on his head, and commenced singing a few Chinese words which he had frequently heard repeated in a temple. The officer was so pleased with this procedure, that he turned round to the soldiers, and ordered them to carry him back to the city. All the rest were placed at short distances from each other on their knees, their feet in irons and hands manacled behind their backs, thus waiting for the executioners, who went round, and with a kind of two-handed sword cut off their heads without being laid on a block. Afterwards their bodies were thrown into one grave, and their heads stuck up in cages on the sea shore. It is said that a violent tempest burst over Tai-wan during the day of the massacre, destroying houses, uprooting trees, and flooding the streams which fed the eity from the hills. Great numbers of the inhabitants were swept away in the rushing waters, others were buried in the ruins of their homes, and it is believed that upwards of two thousand persons perished in the storm. . Takao is about twenty-two miles from Tai-wan, and Ape Hill, a peak of a thousand feet high, points to the entrance of the harbour. *But large vessels cannot ap- proach any nearer than a mile off shore. The inside anchorage is gained through a deep chasm about eighty feet wide, a cleft in the hilly range which faces the sea, running north and south. The passage, however, will only admit small European craft and native junks to the harbour behind the hills. Takao is not unlike a Malay village, but its inhabitants are people of Chinese descent. Groves of tall bamboos and banyan trees shade many of the habitations of the little settlement; the country at this point, and round the large lagoon which forms the inside harbour, is well cultivated. In formation, the hills about Takao, resemble the crater of a volcano, but no traces of such action exist. At one time large apes fre- quented the crags at the back of the village, but they have disappeared, leaving only their name behind. On 1 the hillside, near the gea, is a solitary grave, and the inscription records that an English captain and his wife, murdered thirty miles to the southward, were "buried about this spot' 185—." The stone was broken, and when we last saw it the lettering was almost obliter- ated.

Tam-sui is a port of large trade, carried on with the mainland by' means of Chinese junks, the exports being vegetable oils, camphor, and camphor wood. The scenery around the harbour is imposing; well wooded uplands terminate in a mountainous range- nearly three thousand feet above the sea. A road extends from Tam-sui to Kee- lung, which we have travelled, and between the two places the country is exceedingly rich in views of great natural beauty. Kee-lung is on the northern extremity of the island, the entrance to the port being guarded by rocky ridges extending seaward in various directions. The slopes of the hills, which almost surround the harbour, are under cultivation, with sintimits thickly wooded; and the scene is dotted with occasional temples and official habitations. But few Europeans reside at Kee-lung, and as at Tam-sui, they are mostly in the service of the Chinese Govern- ment. Coal is abundant in the neighbourhood bf Kee- lung, and considerable quantities are shipped thence to different points of the mainland, but the Chinese are slow to realise the great importance of developing such resources of national wealth. In the neighbourhood of Kee-lung, at the harbour mouth, are several interesting caves, penetrating nearly 500 yards into the centre of a hill called the North Peak. We recollect one of these caves was occupied by a Buddhist priest, who had lived over seventy years in his queer abode, but the most fre- quent pilgrim to the old fellow's shrinewas the foreigner. ; It is believed that the Dutch buried treasures in these j caves in the seventeenth century, and perhaps the foreign visitor has a faint hope of being some day sub- stantially rewarded! During the occupanCy of Formosa by the Chinese, they have not disturbed the aborigines dwelling in the wilds of the mountainous range to the eastward and on the south-east coast of the island. These mountain tribes , have always assumed an independent attitude, not quite ' agreeable to their neighbours; and really the Chinese, as , well as other nations, know but very little about them. j They regard all strangers with equal aversion, and, as a matter of fact, they have not hesitated to murder ship- I wrecked persons cast on their shores. Yet, while thee ,
"Oh. George, I'm ashamed of you rubbing your lips like that after that dear little girl has given you so sweet a kiss." "I'm not rubbing it off, nurse. I'm rubbing it in.

As it is not putting on the gown that makes the scholar, but the inward habits of the mind, so it is not putting on an outward -walk of profession that makes a Christian, but the inward grace of the heart. EXTRAORDINARY FREAK OF NATURE. —A lad, hailing from Luchnow, a Bajpoot Hindoo, aged 13 yeqrs, is stated to be exhibiting himself in Suddar Bazaar. He has one kead attached to two bodies. Each trunk is alive to the touch, and each set of limbs work together in unison, per- Inning the same office at the same time; this is the same with the organs of each trunk. The lad gathers up the front limbs and carries them along in moving about. His mental faculties seem intact. An enterprising Parsee gentle- man has advanced the lad's father a thousand rupees in ex- pectation of the success of the exhibition in Poona. In B Anbay several thousand rupees were collected.

People.starils by their barbarism and hostilttfitheY areptpresented as honest, without deception, and faith- ful to a Promise. Shyness is a marked feature with all uncivilised beings, and it forms perhaps the greatest barrier to a familiar iptercourse with them; but when that is overcome, the savage is not so much of a savage after all, even as we have met hint on his native moun- tains. So with the Formosans; and while many atroci- ties are laid at their door, perhaps in the contact with civilisation the savage palm is not always stained with the worst misdeeds.

_ As we have stated, the territory of the aborigines was sealed to strangers, and certainly very little really trust- worthy information of the tribes had beer/ gathered before 1867. In that year General Le Gendre, formerly United States Consur to Amoy, visited Formosa, and put himself in communication with the savages. At first he was refused a landing.; but a second attempt he made, litter in the year, met with success, and almost unat- tended the General ventured into the interior to a con- ference with the chiefs e the eighteen tribes: His object was to obtain a promisO that the savages would re-Nect the lives of white men and, women who should be cast by shipwreck on their shores. Tokitok, the recognised Ileader of the eighteen chiefi,,ultimately gave the desired, ' promise, and there is no reason to believe that it was broken, at all events during his lifetime. A,f ter Tokitok's death the chiefs followed an independent course of action, and though we have knowledge of subsequent Imurders, still it Is almost certain that only the Botan and Kusukut tribes resumed their barbarous impulses against I shipwreckedlpeople. Indeed, if it was not for these II contentions among the tribes who recondt. se no external authority over their wild natures, the Chinese would 'really. have: a very harassing time of it. Although at One time marrying among the Chinese and still:fre- quently mating with the half-breedi, the aborigines have an intense hatred. of the Chinese; and the latter have something more than a common dead' of the mountain savages. Skullsdecorate many hnts• in several of the villages; and the grim tokens account for occasional raids on the far scattered settlements* away from the towns on the coast line, occupied by. the people of Chinese descent. General Le Gendre gained the cons.' dence of the savages and we know that his name is one of peculiar charm to, them, so we acklbee- his testimon7. somewhat describing their condition. "As- a people, the condition of the Fbrmosan aborigines- of the present' day is this: It is true that their timeis chiefly taken up with hunting, but,unlike the American Indians, they do not live a -wandering life, and they are far from de- pending entirely upon:the proceeds of the 'chase for sub- sistence. Those of the men who, through age or in-. firmity, become unfit for the arduous exertion of hunt- ing, spend their time in the fields, tilling the-ground with ' the women, and raising millet and other food for the ' maintenance of the tribe. The women also weave cloth. They live together in, villages; in houses bnilt either of split bamboo or else- of slate in a style peculiar to them- selves. They do not live together as a nation united under one king,; buteach tribe, or collection of tribes, constitutes a free organisation, each member contributing to the maintenance of the commonwealth, acting either u:nder a hereditary chief or under officer elected by the people. They believe in u Supreme Being, and also, like the Chinese, an the occult influences of nature; but they worship no idols. They have now no system of writing, but have a high appreciation of eloquence, prudence, and wisdom, which,. as a rule, are the only titles among them that render a man eligible to public office. They are by nature exceedingly civil and polite, and would be inclined to hospitably receive strangers had they not been ren- dered extremely suspicions of them by the harsh and cruel treatment received 'at the hands of the Chinese since the expulsion of the Dutch from the island in the seventeenth century; but for a hundred years past they have strictly and persistently closed their territory to them."

The mountain tribes are supposed to be of Malayan or Polynesian origin, but it is not unlikely they are descen- dants of the Lew-chew islanders who held Formosa pre- vious to the Japanese occupancy of the island. They have fine graceful figures,. good features, and wear long hair; and in their bearing, have an independence and dash not found among the Chinese. Both sexes chew betel-nut incessantly, and their persistent indulgence in the habit is their worst personal disfigurement, for the red saliva discolours the whole of the mouth and lips. Otherwise the women have some claims to good looks, and not disfigure their features as is so often the case with Asiatics; they pay particular attention to their hair, coiling it like a diadem round their head. They occasionally wear head ornaments qf flowers and coloured slips of cloth twisted in their hair. The marriage cere- mony is a simple one; the hand of the lady is placed by her father into the palm of the suitor, and a general family merry-making terminates the rite. :The acceptance of a present is also sufficient to tie the wedding knot, and it may be as easily set aside. One very excellent trait is their respect for old people; the grey hairs of age are safe everywhere, among all the tribes. They are fend of frolic, and .indulge in rude graceful dances and wild games of skill and strength, such as one would expect of men who almost live by the chase. A few years since Formosa was the subject of dispute between the Chinese and Japanese Governments, and for a time war between the two countries was imminent. The Japanese sent a military expedition to the south-east coast of the island; and, as a conclusion, we will briefly chronicle the cause and the result of that plucky step. The near view of, Formosa had for many years been regarded with apprehension by the tempest-tossed mariner; death was the fate of castaways driven there by the calamities of the ocean. Perhaps, occasionally, the aborigines were charged with crimes they had never committed; and certainly in several instances the Chinese themselves practised piracy and murder thereabouts. The only certainty was that no one escaped; men and women of all nations were slaughtered. In December, 1871, a large trading and fishing junk from the Riu Kiu Islands was driven ashore on the east coast of Formosa, and fifty-four Japanese sailors were massacred; some others escaped and carried the tidings to their people. The Japanese sent a special envoy to China to demand punishment of the savages, but the Chinese Government disclaimed responsibility for the territory where the murders were committed. Failing to impress the Chinese with the importance of subduing the savage nature of the aborigines, and rendering the shores of Formosa safe for the voyager, the Japanese themselves resolved to act in the interests of humanity, and accordingly, in May, 1874, they landed a force on the island, at Liangkiao Bay. Later in the month, the famous Japanese general, Saigo, arrived with additional troops, and thereafter followed a series of movements, excursions, and skirmishes in the interior, which soon brought the savages to understand their helpless condition when opposed to an organised force as well used as themselves to mountain welfare. The Botans and Kusukuts, certainly the most hostile of the tribes, were the last to own themselves beaten; and witti their submission the next step of the expedition had tb be considered. Perhaps the Japanese intended to construct stations for the safety of the ship- wrecked on those wild shores at least for a time, until the savages fully comprehended what was required of them. Saigo contemplated introducing, improved methods of agriculture among the mountain tribes. But trouble had meanwhile sprung up between the Govern- ments of China and Japan, for the former now insisted that her territory had been invaded; and fob a time the two countries were facing each other with hostile intent —perhaps not a very decided attitude on the part of China, a great deal too much bluster and equivocation ; but certainly Japan would not leave her good work un- finished, and otherwise she was well able to stand up against any serious action of her giant foe. Happily, how- ever, blows did not fall. At a certain stage the English Minister at the Chinese Court, Sir Thomas Wade, was asked to negotiate with the Japanese, and ultimately a peaceful arrangement was effected. The Chinese Government paid an indemnity, and acknowledged Japan justified in the act of occupation; the latter to withdraw her troops, and China to be responsible for the safety of the Formosan coast thereafter. In thus championing the rights of humanity. in the face of many obstructions, it is no small satisfaction to believe that the patient and consistent attitude of Japan triumphed over the cunning and chicanery of the Chinese authorities. Whatever might have been the result of hostilities between the two 4 countries we venture no conjecture; we are content to read the one important lesson out of her history, that Japan, acting with wise promptitude, cleared the Eastern Seas of a terror that was common to men of all nations navigating those treacherous waters.

A RIMARICABLE FAMILY.—In the reign of King William 111. there lived at Ipswich, in Suffolk, a family which, from the number of peculiarities belonging to it, was die- tinguished by the name of the Odd Family. Every event, remarkably good or bad, happened to this family in an odd year, or on an odd day of the month, and every one of them had something odd in his or her person, manner, and be. havionr. The very letters of their Christian names al vays happened to be of an odd number. The huslJand's name was Peter, and the wife's was Rake); they had seven children, all boys—vi., Solomon, Roger, James, Matthew, Jonas David, and Ezekiel. The husband bad but one leg, and his wife but one arm. Solomon was born blind of his left eye, and Roger lost his right eye by accident. James had his left ear pulled off by a boy in a quarrel, and Matthew was born with only three fingers on his right hand. !Jonas had a stump foot, and David was humpbacked. All , these, except David, were remarkably short, and Ezekiel was 6 feet 2 inches high at the age of 13. The stump-footed Jonas and humpbacked David got wives of fortune, but no ' girl wonld listen to ihe addresses of the rest. The bus- ban I's h tir was black as jet, and the wife's remarkably white; yet every one of the children were red-haired. The husband had the peculiar misfortune to fall into a deep saw pit, where he was starvrd to death in the year 1701 and the wife, refusing all kinds of sustenance, died in five days after him. In the year 1703 Ezekiel enlisted as a Grenadier, and although he was afterwards wounded in 23 places, be recovered. Roger, James, Matthew, Jonas, and David died at different places en the same day in the year 1713, and Solomon and Ezekiel were drowned together in creasing the 'themes in the year 1723. _

HOUSE OF COMMONS.— te lEDNESMT. The speaker took the chair at, o'clock. ..,rtelity.minutes after twelve

_ THE SHIP r• eatiAL hLL rassEn.--The Manchester Ship I Canal El" eell wait brought up and considered.—On the motion 01 Sir C. FORSTER standing orders 22a and 243 were sus- ' 'ended, and the Bill was read a third time, the Queen's consent on behalf of the Crown and Duchy of Lancaster to be signified. The Bill passed its final stage in the louse of Commons amidst a general cheer. ENGLAND AND EGYPE.—On the order for the third read- ing of the Consolidated Fund (Appropriation) Bill, Mr. LABOCCHERE moved a resolution declaring that the Bill should not be proceeded with until the Government had ex- nlained to the House its policy with regard to Egypt and the conditions under whi ch the recent guaranteed loan was issued. After some remarks from Sir George Campbell and Sir W. Lawson, the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said be freely recognised the right of the House to asks for explanations as to the proceedings of the Government. Everything that had been done during the last five years had heaped up obligations in regard to Egypt which could not be evaded, and whilst the Government recognised the rights and inter- ests of the other Powers in Egypt it would endeavour to act in concert with them. The goodwill of the Sultan had been too much ignored in the past, but the Government con- sidered this esseatial to a satisfactory settlement. He could not state with advantage the precise instructions given to Sir kf D. Wolff, but the object of his mission was to put the Egyptian Government upon a footing with respect to the external defence of the country, its internal administration, and its financial position, such as would give freedom to its indepennent actron in the future'. To effect a satisfactory settlement would be a work of stime, and it would be for the public advantage to declare toethe world that we intended to remain in Egypt until this was accomplished. For the arrangement with respect to the loan—which had been accepted by Parliarmait the Government was not solely responsible, having to act so as to meet the views of the other Powers. The greatest dan• ! gers might have arisen if the issue of the lean had been any longer delayed, and under the circumstances the Govern- ment had made the best arrangement in its power.— Lord HARTINGTON said he had no complaint to make of the statement of the Chancellor of the. lx- chequer, although it was in vague and general terms, but he did not see in what degree the present Government had assumed a more definite attitude in regard to Egyptian trite!, than that of whi9h tby had compleined so much. Eke thought, moreover, that thei character ttild afol of Sir H. Wolff's mission should be accurately defined and understood, and that the Chancellor of the Exchequer should have deellred that part of the intention of Her Majesty/a ClotrOeiittiet to upset the Khedive or In Wad ho Pftiee to any lkft'gue against the existing GoVattitifint thero.—Mr. ihtdiawm said there was no intentien ott the part of Her Maje Sty's Government to withhold that support from the Khediye which he had received from the late Govern- ments—The amendmint was negatived. Mr. ARNOLD next called attention to the Royal Commis- sion ou the Depression of Trade, aid asked what was the at- titude of the Government as to the policy of free imports, on which the supply of cheap food to the working-cheeses so largely depended.—A number of other questions were raised by various members, but eventually the Appropria- tion Bill was read a third time and passed.---'fbe Federal Council of Australasia Bill and the Secretary for Scotland Bill were also read a third time and passed.--Before the adjournment of the House the Universities (Scotland) Bill and the Factory Acts (Extension to Shops) Bill were with- drawn.
• The- House adjourned at ten minutes to Ms. HOUSE OF LORDS,—Tlttrastult.

The Ltrd 01-ia-nc-e-lle; took his'ieit at four o'clock. TKE SHIP CANAL Brm.--The Royal assent was given by Commission to 56 public and private bills, the following being amongst the number :—Manchester Ship Canal, ,Modical Relief Diequalifipations Removal, Bankruptcy (Office Accommodation), Public Health (Members and Offices), Parliamentary Elections (Corrupt Practices), and Lunacy Acts Amendment. The Lords Commissioners were the Lord Chancellor, Lord Cranbrook, and E irl 13eautharup. MrS4xmaxxors.—Lord EmateirroNs moved -to amend an Irish Provisional Order Bill for the purpose of requiring the Dublin Corporation to supply 25 gallons of water per bead per day, in lieu of 20 gallons, to the outlying town- ships.—After some discussion, their lordships on a division rejected the amendment by 20 to 19.—The Poor Law Unions (Officers) (Ireland) Bill, the Evidence by Commission Bill, , the Telegraphs Act Amendment Bill, and the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill were read a third time and passed. Their lordships adjourned at twenty minutes past six o'clock.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock, QUESTIONS.-Mr. Balfour. answering a quettion about cholera precautions, said that, besides having forbidden the impartation of rags from Spain, the Local Government Board had under consideration the question whether they ought not under present circumstances to prohibit such im- portation from France also. In the cottese of answers given by Ministers as to the business of the House, it was stated that it was not likely that the Burgh Police and Health (Scotland) Bill would be proceeded with. The Chancellor of the Exchequer said that Lord ildesleigh would make a ststement in the House of Lords on Monday or Tuesday neat on the subject of the Trade Commission. THE INDIAN BUDGE I.

The Heine haring gone into Committee on the Indian Revenue Accounts, Lord It. CHURCHILL me& his Budget ! etatemente He said the revised estimate for the year 1884-5 ' showed a deficit of znopoo, Mete Ld of a surplus, as esti- mated. The revised estimate was worse than the original one by the sum of £1,029,000. Thera could he no doubt that the chief cause of the falling off wee duo to the great depression and the diminished rice trade with ,Britiern Burmah. The Budget for the corrent year had been estimated by the Government of India in March last as follows :—Rstimated revenue, £72,1)9e,000 ; expendi- ture, £71,582,000; or to give a surplus of 4;508.000. The total expenditure not pcovided for in the March Budget was lx,sacioo ; and as the Government of 'lndia thought an increase of taxation in the current year 'would be most un- desirable, it Wki determined to inset the extra and nnpro- , vided-for expenditure by economy and by overdrawing their account. They tad effected a weving against 111, revenue of the year of £1,797,000. To all in- tents and purposes the famine insurance fund had been swallowed up. The whole 'condition of India political and fieenrial, had been suddenly changed, and it had not been changed for the better. 'lndia had ceased to be isolated from all contact with 'European 'Powers. Indian credit had fallen by eight ne nine per cent. which indicated a change of serious importance. Fie estimated, moreover, the permanent increase in the military charge at two mil- lions a year. It could' hardly be 1,839 than one and a half million. Themroposed increase ofethe Indian army would necessitate werequivalent' increase of,Britieh troope in India. i,Hie lordship then proceeded. to condemn the Government of Lord Ripon for not looking ahead.—Mr. J. K. excess said this waerthe first occasion to his knowledge wheneunder cover of a financial statement, wild partisan attack had ' been made en a late Viceroy. A ROYAL HOLIDAY.—The following is the way in which the Crown Prince and Princess of Prusiia are eri:oying their holiday in Switzerland :—" The time is he morning of July 30 ; the place is the little Swiss village of Ander- matt, .5,000f1. above the sea, among the mountains; lender- neath is the St. Crothard tunnel. A rushing torrent pours through the middle of the village, crossed by a low stone bridge. On one side a steep rock c tete its shadow over the green sward closely cropped, and everywhere else theloods of sunshine gild and glorify the picturesque old hoases and the rugged street. In this one shady spot by the, roadside a family party have established themselves to sketch. There are three sweet young girls in simple blue dresses, with straw hats, intently working at their drawing, sitting on the grass with their sketch-books on !their laps. There is an older lady made more comfortable with two chairs and an. easel, sketching in oils. The-e is a man in a wide straw hat with a fair beard, anxiously attending to her wants and studying her comfort. A little further off a gentleman holds by a chain a beautiful greyhound. The carriages trot along the road, the coachmen crack their whips, lact none of the party ever look up. Thee- are too intent upon their work. 'SALVATION ARMY .D;4,MONSTRATION.
'THE "MODERN BABYLON "REVELATIONS.

The St. Helens corps of the Salvation Army held a series of demonstrations on Saturday and Sunday. On the first- named day the well-known "General" Booth, the founder and leader of the "Army " morement, paid his ,first visit to St. Helens, and his arrival created great interest through- out the town. It had been announced that he would arrive .at the railway station about four o'clock, and at that hour a large concourse of people assembled in the vicinity await- ing his arrival. -About half-past four the train from Lou- don drew up in the station, the entrance to which was blocked by the railway officials and police officers. The "General," on stepping from the compartment, was received by Major Sowerby, of Liverpool, the " divisional officer," who was attired from head to foot in a bright scarlet uni- form, with a helmet to match. As General Booth stepped into a" war chariot "—an open carriage covered with a for cloth, drawn by a pair of "greys "—a "royal salute" of cheers and " hallelujahs" was given, while there was also some slight hissing. A procession was then formed. In front rod. two mounted "officers," while Major Sowerby took his seat in the " war chariot " with the " general." About fifty members of the "army" took part in the pro- ceeeion,b.rnich was led up by the brass band of the St. Helens corps. As they paraded the principal streets of the town large crowds of people assembled to witness the de- monstration. In the evening a great demonstration led by the " general," woo held in the Volunteer Hall, and there WAS a large attendance. In an address "General Booth reviewed the work of the army since its eatathistament about 20 years ago. He said that for the first. 12 years nothing remarkable took place—it was fotuadation work—but during the last eight...years the num- ber of corps bad increased from .25 to 1,000, paid officers from 35 to 2,750, and periodicals from one with a circulation of 12,000 or 15,000 a month to eighteen separate religious newspapers with a circulation of half a million copies per week. Tneir profit on the newspaper department, uniform department, Jac., was something like £7,000, and every penny of it had been put in the Lord's treasury to en- .able them to roll the Lord's war chariot along. He (the General) was full of hope that they would see far greater things in the future. He was lost in wonder and amaze- ment almost every day of his life to see the marvellous op- portunities stretching out before them. Their colours were flying not only in this country, but in eighteen other coun- tries and colonies. Amongst other things the army mem- bers were adapting themselyes especially to helping dis- charged criminals, and they-had been remarkably success- ful in the work. lie trusted the time was not far distant when they would have an officer in every police court and every court of justice in the land, and when magistrates and judges might say to habitual criminals, You have been here many a time. We will adopt another plan. We shall give you a week's imprisonment and six months with the Salvation Army." (Applause.) He believed that time would come. Refer- ring to the recent revelations mode by the Pall Mall Gazette, General Booth said they were of a most painful character, showing that there had been a system of betray- ing young girls, drawing them away in ignorance or com- pulsion, and blighting and ruining them for this world aod for the world to come. Those revelations had been mode and verified. In the fitst instance their truthfulness was denied. It was said that they were not true, but the imagin- ation of some penny-a-liner written in some garret for bread. The commission, composed of the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Bishop of London; Cardinal Manning, the Recorder of London, and Mr. Samuel Morley, had a good many sittings, examined witnesses, and had issued their ver- dict that those revelations were substantially true. The evidence bad not been published; if it had been it would have shown that villanies were practiced which would make the hair of every time-hearted Englishman

stand on end, In fact, s.) shucking wire they that it was said they ware too vile to be publishe;„ If no, the General emphasised how vile they mug ha ben be to be practised. However, they had been practised,, Wed something must be done to put a stop to them. Sorne..hing had been done Oa Friday night a substantial portion of the bill before Parliament received approval., buc be trusted other improve- ments would be made in it Odom it became law. They had made the protective age sixtem They oneht to make an effort to induce the House of Lords to make it seventeen, and aftersvar.is to try to rnake it eiahtecn, and then twenty-one, and then to make seduction altogether a crime punishable by the law of the tend. But the Salvation Army intended to try to do something more, and he would on Sunday afternoon bri,lit before them a great scheme. Let them go on trying to 'cave the people. (Applause.

; WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB. ; A Meeting Of the committee of this club was held On Wednesday evening at the club room, White Bull, Horsemarket-street, Warrington, Mr. Marsh. presiding.—The first business on the agenda paper was to further consider the rent question and to hear communications from landowners thereon.— The SECRETARY (Mr. H. T. Stelfox) said that a letter had been received from Mr. A. C. Talbot stating that the communication of the club had. been received, and was under consideration. Metara. Peace and Ellis, of Wigan, wrote on behalf of Mrs. Bankes, of Winstanley, that Mrs. Bankes had. Ireceived an application from some of the Winstead ley tenants for a reduction of their rents. The matter was under cousideration, and they hoped that an arrangement would ultimately be made which would meet the justice of each case. These replies, the Secretary said, in addition to the one from Colonel Legh read at the last meeting, were the whole of the direct answers from landovvners. Beyond that there had certainly been an intimatiors from one landowner to whom a rent memorial was forwarded, but it was not a direct intimation to the club. It had, however, had the desired effect, that the landowner—Sir George Chetwynd—had granted a reduction of 10 per eent, to his tenant farmers. (Hear, hear.) Owing to the apparent failure of the rent memorial to obtain from the land- owners that , which the tenantry of the Warrington district considered to be abso- lutely necessary for the well being-- of their business, it was thought desirable now that some further steps should be taken to press the matter home. They were told that they could trust Ito the good relations and the kindly feeling that existed, between landlord and tenant to secure everything that the tenant farmer required. It was therefore necessary that whenever possible the ten- ant farmers should approach the landowners in order that it might not be said that they did not try their best to get what advantage might accrue from that kindly feeling. It was for the committee to consider whether they could recommend the members of the club to sign private memorials of the , t3nantry on each estate, or recommend the ten- antry to go in a body to the landowners with their own private memorials. The matter would then be placed before each landowner,in a clear, decisive% manner, and the amount of friendly feeling existing between them and the tenantry would be fairly ascertained. No doubt some landowners might object to being pressed by a Club, but if their tenantry approached them that objection was removed. In answer to a ques- tion, Mr. Stelfox said that between 40 and 50 land- lords had been communicated with.—The CHAIR,. MAN thought that there was no doubt that they were in as bad a fix as ever they were before.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that he did not anticipate many direct replies, because he thought that it was inten- ded that the matter should be left in such a way that those receiving the communications could either reply or not, Still they expected to see better 'effects. It was, however, more intended as a means of paving the way for the tenants to approach the Ilandlords on their own acceunt, and to make it 'easier for them to do so.—Mr. FERGUSON said that they must bear it in mind that all the members of an estate might not be members of the club,• and perhaps only a small section would agree with the arrangement suggested.—The SECRETARY said that he believed that the action of the club was being followed by the entire tenant farmers in the dis- trict, who entirely approved of it. Some did not like to join the club because of the landlords and agents. There was a large proportion of tenant farmers in Cheshire who were under obligations to the landlords in consequence of the agricultural de- pression. Consequently they appeared rather a fillii.ic of joining the club.—The CHAIRMAN' said that se, long as a farmer had backbone in him his landlord, as a rule, would take it out of him. It was a mis- take for farmers who could not pay their way to stay lin the farms. If they could not get their rents re- duced let them leave their farms; there were plenty of others to be had.—Finally, after a long discus- sion, it was decided that the secretary draw up a isecond memorial, to be sent from the club to land-. I lords, for consideration at a future meeting.—lre answer to the agricultural programme sent to candi- dates for Parliament, Mr. I. S. Leadam, Liberal can- didate for the Altrincham Division, writing from the Reform Club, S.W., said it was impossible to answer categorically" Yes" or "No " to the quea- tions put. For example, a pledge to vote for the election of county government boards would have been satisfied had the members supported, during the last Conservative Government, the bill of Mr. Sclater-Booth, which, in fact, christened I quarter sessions as county boards, and gave the merest figment of concession to the demands of those who desired that county boards should be frankly represented. Similarly, an affirmative might be. given to the third question, and the elected member might thereupon vote for any permissive and nuga- tory bill like that of 1875. His desire was to leave no loophole for evasion, and to set forth the manner in which it was sought to attain their objects, at the same time defining with more precision the agri- cultural reforms which he had long advocated. He Suggested that candidates should be invited to ad- dress meetings of the club.—The Hon. Tatton Egerton, candidate for the Knutsford division, wrote expressing willingness to answer any questions put to him at a public meeting, but declining to send. written answers to a private association outside the division.—The Secretary reported answers given at a public meeting by Mr. John Brookes, one of the candidates written to.—lt was not considered ad- visable to ask any candidates to address the club. —This was all the business of interest.

div.p: ALARMING RAILWAY COLLISION AT
CHESTER.

On Monday morning two excursion trains, one from St. Helens and the other from the North Staffordshire line, arrived in Chester about 7-30. When approaching Boole- lane junction they collided, the St. Helen train dashing on the same line ea the North Stafford train. Three carriages of the former train were thrown on to the embankment and smashed. Both trains were en route for Llandudno and car- ried large cargoes of passengers. The .passengers in both trains were severely shaken. but fortunately no lives were lost or injuries of a serious nature sustained. The passen- gers who are most seriously injured are Mrs. Belfield, of Mow Cop :David Goodhead, of Wolstsnton ; Mr. Alrllwood,, of Newcastle, Staffordshire; and Mr. John Clayton, of Ash.. field, Newcastle. Mr. Clayton was taken to the Chester Infirmary, and the other passengers complain of bruises and shocks to the system. Other trains were procured, and the. excursionists, who had been detained for several hours, pro- ceeded on their journey. The accident caused a large amount of excitement.

It was stated by the officials that one train was proceeding along the Crewe line, and the other along the Manchester line. The scene of the catastrophe was on Monday visited by hundreds of persons, the bridge over the railway at !he spot being crowded. The excursion and ordinary traffic was muchater hlt interferedNfr the line being partially birchd- L e orwnieand his officials bad arranged the arri- val and departure of trains, and traffic was proceeding as well as could be expected under the circumwances. A bream- down gang was engaged at the place where the accident occurred.

The passengers in the St. Helens train were severely shaken, and the tender was forced off the metals and thrown across both the up and down lines. It is stated that the driver o the St. Helens train alleges that when he came in eight of t'mr Nortn Staffordshire train the impetus on this heavy train ,VaS SO grelt that the brakes were powerless to nrevent a collision. Conslderable datrnage was done to the permanent wAy,and the trains which were blocked accumn. lited, but in about two bouts the tender was replaced on the metals Ur the Chester breakdown gang, and traffic was te. sumed.

Several of the Widnes passengers by the excursion train which came into collisien near Chester Station, on Monday, hare been intgrviewed. Mr. William Butler, of Princess.. street, Widnes, a foreman in the employ of Mr. Lama, proprietor of tte Widnes Iron Dram Works, made a state- ment to the following rffectz—" I W,t:i one of the passengers in the train which collided at Chester Junction on Monday. We started, from the London and North-Weetern station here at twenty minutes past *ix a.m. cm Monday for an excursion to Llandudno. t should say there Were 100 pa. sourer, at least from Widnes. All went safe until we got to Chester Junction, and then our train got up to the other, which was Cu excursion train from Staffordshire, and ran right into it. There were two carriages in the Staffordshire train upset,and one carriage in our train testi knocked off the line. Of coursa the collision caused great consternatiou amongst the passengers, but no one in our train was Injured. though Passengers were thrown from their seats. severallwasinothe fifth carriage from the engine, and to me the shock was very slight. It seemed to nie only a bit of a jerk. Mr. Rollason was in the carriage next the engine, and though it was knocked off the line be is not hurt. Soots after the collision occurred the porters came and told us to go up to the station, where we found another train waiting to take us to Llandudno. We were delayed about an boar altogether. All the passengers had a miraculous esca.,e from death. The women and children appeiired to be ter:le his' frightened, and the former did an alarming amount of screaming."

At the Liverpool Assizas, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Manisty, John Pearson (33), labourer, was indicted on the charge of having. at Parr, in the borough of St. Helens, on the 18th May last, feloniously administered to Sarah Alice Pearson a quantity of a certain poison called oxalid acid, with intent ,in as doing then and thereby feloniously, wikfully, and of his malice aforethought to kill .and merder her. There were also charges against the pri- soner of having administerel the same poison to Margaret Ann Pearson and Maria Pearson with intent to murder them on the 18th of May, but the first charge was only gone into. Mr. Watson appeneed for the prosecution, and the prisoner was not represented.—Prisoner, it eee.ned, resided in Wood-etteet, St. Helens, and some little time ago his wife died. He appeared to be in very distressed circum- stances, and Was left with three little children, the eldest of whom, Sarah Alice Pearson, was nine years of age. On the morning of the 18th of May this child came downstairs, when the met her father, teho had a cup in his hands containing some liquid. The prisoner went up- emirs, and soon afterwards returned, still hold- ing the cup, the contents of which he offered to hie O&M daughter, saying, "This will do your cough good." The girl drank Borst of the stuff, but she felt it irritating and burning, and it made her vomit. It the jury were satisfied that what the prisoner did with (he cup and liquid upstairs was similar to what he did downstairs, then it showed that he had done a deliberate act. Another cir- cumstance occurred, and this was that whet the eldest giel was drinking the ntixture some of it was Pplit on her drepea, which was shown to these who zubsequenteY law her. This happened before ten o'clock in the morning, and at that hour the prisoner called upon a neighbour named lames Gee, and said, "I have poisoned Came' Gee said, "Poisoned what?" and prisoner answered, "The three chil- dren." Gee afterwarde received a nete frcm his wife writ- ten by the prisoner, which said:—" Geee Please write and let my brother, Lawrence Peerson of Barateee, know. Only sorry they are not dead." A Mre. Trrers and a Mrs. Marsh came to the assistance of the children and gave them emetics. Prisoner at the time wee sittirtgby himself, and, upcn being asked by the women what he Lai done it for, he did not speak, hut afterwards said thet he had given his children exalic aciC. Dr. Cesey, of Stet.cn, in the meantime easibreught in, who found tat poison 'had, been administered. The eldeet girl was then in danger, but the emetic tint had been given her mitigated the etects of the poison. It was shown ttat prisoner tad purchased two pennyworth of emetic acid from Mr. lames Horrocks, an assistant to a IruggisL 'Upon the prisoner being asked why he cornett:4d the act he said, " They must not go to the workhouse;" and when taken into custody by Police-censtable Metcatfe tee said, "It ie a pity they are not dead." Prisoner made a statement to the jury in Which be seta he purchased an (lance of oxalic acid on the flBth of May and partly dissolved it in hot water rued left it to cool. tie had a private purpose for it and had no intention of giving it to the children. He placed it on the table, and 'being excited throegls 'something taking place previously, he made a mistake when the children upstairs asked for a drink of water, sad he gave them the wrong •cup. The two children then lay down quietly and he came downstairs and gave his other daeghtee some. He said teeer, "Ve ill you take some of this water, it wilt make your ceagh better." Then she commenced crying and, said it butlett her throat. Ile then went across to Gee's and told them what be had done.—rhe jury found the prisoner guilty of Iministering this poison with intent to murder, and hie Lordship, in passing sentence, said the prisoner had beet found guilty of the greatest crime next to that of murder, and had with deliberate intentioe tried to pat an end to the lives of his children. There might have been distress of which he was not acquainted, bet he was sorry to say that the evidence I was so coriciusiveHeat he was hound to *pee a terrible sen- tence which, unless there be circumstances to mitigate the ' offence, RAI the least that could be passed in such a case, as it was next to murder. That sentence was twenty years' ' penal servitude. Upon heariag this the crisoner became quite excited, anew up his arms, and loudly exclaimed, "1 I shall never do it, my lord."

THE TRIAL OF RIEL.-VERDICT LND SENTENCE DEATH.

REGINA, SATERDAY.—The trial of Riet was concluded to- day. fhe Judge read the evidence, and in charging the jury directed them to find a verdict of "Guilty," unieen they believed the prisoner to be irresporsealy insane during the rebellion. The summing-up lasted four hours. The jury retired to consider their verdict, and in their absence Rid knelt down ill the dock and prayed audibly and fer- vently. After an hour's deliberation the jury returned into court and stated, in reply to the usual interrogatories, that they found the prisoner guilty, but recommended him to mercy. The prisoner was quite unmoved when the verdict was announced.

REGINA, SVEDAY.—RieI has been sentenced to be hanged at Regina on the 18th of September. Notice has been given of appeal. REGINA, TT:TES:MT.—The trial of 26 half-breeds, who were made prisoners during the recent rebellion in the North- west, took place this afternoon. The prisoners, among whom were Riel's counsellors, pleaded guilty to the charge of trea- son-felony. Sentence was postponed until after the con? clusion of the murder trials. It is believed, however, that the prisoners will be treated with clemency by the Crown. Four of them hare already been discharged. Eci YET AND THE SOUDAN.—REPOIL LTD DEATH OF OSMAN DIG:11A. CAIRO, MONDAS —Major-General Grenfall telegraphs that an Arab has arrived at Korosko from Berber, who reports that the rebel force which attacked Lassala on June 15 and R 3 consisted of Osman Digm t's men. The Arab further states that Osman Digma is dead.
Cern°, TVESDAY.—A. telegram has been received from Major Chsrmaide contradicting the reported death of Osman Digna. THE CHOLERA SCOURGE STILL SPREADING.— OU rEiREAK AT MARSEILLES.

num% MOZWAY.—The official cholera bulletin reports 3,807 cases and 1.361 deaths in Spain yesterday. hlansuiLLEs, IVIONDAY.—To-dav, for the first time, in- form ttion respecting the outbreak of cholera here is al- lowed to be telegraphed. The disease first appeared 801110 days since. The average number of deaths daily is 10 to 20. Yesterday there were 26 deaths. Among the vic- tims is the Consul of Portugal here. Last year the cholera principally attacked ,the poorest classes ; this year it prin- cipally attacks the rich. Since midnight there have been 22 deaths.

TRIESTE, MONDAY.--IE consequence of the reporte4 ap- pearance of cholera in Marseilles, it has been ordered that al! arrivals from French Mediterranean ports, including Algiers, shall be placed under olsservation for ten days before receiv- ;Me', free pratique. The troops in Tonquin. ac- cording to intelligence in the Temps, are being severely tried by dysentery and dangerous fevers. In May the [nor- ' tality among the soldiers was 161, against 41 in May of last year, and during the first fortnight of Jane the deaths aver- aged 12 daily. In view of these facts, the Temps insists that soldiers who have been in Tonquin for 18 months should I be promptly brought home,

What was termed else " bembardment " was continued on Sunday. when the local corr was largely reinforced by con- tingents from Warringtoe, Widnes, Runcorn, te. Their processions through the town were heralded by the band, and their meetiegs in the Volunteer Hall included " Holi- ness feast," "war memories," and "free salvatien," General 13ooth being" in commend all dav:" In the elternoon the " General " referred In a new scheme for the rescue of fallen girls end the de.:ivarance of those in <tenger. In speaking in the -evening Geceral Booth said he would again say eornething•to them about the greet scheme which he had it connection with the recent agitetion in London. They knew very well, be supposed, that theee had been cer- tain revelations made in a Lenden newspaper with regari to the iniquities that had been practised in the ruin of young girls in Lendon, and in some of the large centres of populetion up and down the country. He was corning to believe that them things had been more prevalent in some of tie smaller towns and villages than some of them had any idea of. For a long time the Salvation Army, in its widespread acquaintance eith iniqeity, had been made aware thst certain Of those evds were in progress, but during the lane twelve months, since they went more specially into this department of labour, thoss revelations had been (cede to them very frequently. In fact they (the Army) determined that same desperate effort should be made to obtain relief by an amendment in the law. He spoke of the assistance rendered to the editor of the Pall JIaU Gazdte by the Salvation Army, and west on to say that the House of Commons had done something, but they asked for four things. First, they wanted the age of con- sent raised to 18 years; it had been raised to 16 ; there was a fight for'ls, as the ago of protection. They (the Army) reckoned that a young girl was not sufficiently acquainted with the consequences of iniquity until she came to be 18 years of age, and as she had no power over her property until she was 21, she ought to have no power over her virtue until she was of the same age. The age used to be 13, and before that 12; but these senators of theirs in the House of Commons—they were wonderful men—(laughter) —in •a fit of generosity raised the age to 13, and now to 16—(cheers)—because they were made. He would make them raise the age of conomt to 21. (Cheers.) Another, thing they asked for was the right of search. If a girl under age was taken away to a house of ill-fame for immoral purposes, then the mother, father, or anyone in- terested in the child, should be able to get A search warrant from a magistrece, and search for the girl. At present a parent could not go in'o the house and take out her child. The speaker then gave instances of servants taking lodgings in brothels, and how they were entrapped. Their scheme was to establish an agency that would nave its representa- tive branches in every big town and city where the English language was spoken, and gradually to spread it all over the world. They proposed having a central house of inquiry in the centre of London. Its doors would never be closed, day or night, so that any poor girl could run to it, and she would be safe. By means of this, parents could get to know how their children were getting on in London. They in- tended to establish refuges, which would take in 1,000 girls, in all pats of London, and in some of toe principal towns In the country. They bad set apart their soldiers for a res- cue brigade ; and they proposed to have homes in the Western States of America, to which they could convey the fallen girls and get them situations. (Cheers.) A short prayer was then said, and the meeting closed with a collection.

At a Cabinet Council held on Thursday it was decided that Parliament should be prorogued on Thursday next. THE STRIKE IN THE COTTON TRADE.—At last there is a break in the situation as regards the Oldham strike. On Wednesday Mr. Stott, of Coldhurst Mill, had an interview with his operatives. As the result an agreement has been effected whereby the workpeople resume work on their own terms-5 per cent reduction, concurrent with short time for four days per week. This firm, employing about 500 hands, spins coarse counts, which may be classed as A spe- ciality. THE GENER&L ELECTION—We have received from the Central News a list of the candidates who are seeking elec- tion at the forthcoming General Election, revised down to July 31st. There are 91 seats in England and Wales for which at present there are no Conservative candidates. On the other hand, there are 49 seats where Liberal candidates are wanting. In 11 instances two Conservative candidates are contesting the same seat, while in 35 cases the Liberal interest is split in a similar way. In Scotland there are 30 vacancies for Conservative cantlidates, while the Liberals have only five seats for which no candidate is in the field. In only one case does a Conservative candidate in Scotland threaten to divide the Conservative vets, but with the Liberals there are 14 candidates who are similarily im- perilling their party's ch ances. In Ireland scarcely any steps have been taken for the selection of candidates. The Parnellites have not yet spoken, and in 54 constituencies there are neither Liberal, Conservative, nor flamelike can- didates in the field. MR. FORSTER, M.P., ON PUBLIC ekFFAIRS.-013 Saturday Mr. W. E. Forster delivered a farewell address to the elec- tors of the old constituency of Bradford. lie remarked that the clause in the Lend Act giving fixity of tenure was in- serted at his suggestion. Had he consulted his reputation he would have retired when the Compensation for Distur- bance Bill was thrown out by the Reuse of Lords, and if he had been able with a clear canacieace to: remain M. his post he would have been able to complete the pacification of Ireland. It PM a bitter reflection that had he remained the agitators would have gone on attempting to murder him, and two of his dear frien Is would have been spared. Terrible as those murders were, they saved Ireland. Tne non-renewal of the Crimes Act meant that if anybody corn- muted an agrariain outrage, from murder downwards, it would be almost impossible to convict him. It also meant that the " boycotting pike" would be used. Inasmuch as the Government, with its eyes. open, had allowed the pro- visions against boycotting to lapse, the people. net un- naturally, would pimp to the conclusion that boycotting was not only legal, but permissible. He had great confidence in Lord Carnarvon, but the speeches of Lord Randolph Churchill and his colleagues would not render the task of governing with the ordinary law an easier one. Mr. Forst r declared himself in favour of strong land laws, local option within limits, and local self 'government, -against the State taking the land from one man and giving it to another. ano against cumulative taxation. With reference to foreign affairs he had not entire conAdence in pdr. Gladstone, and he objected to the" one man " policy:-
