Bank Holiday was wisely turned to account at Warrington and at Runcorn by demonstra- tions in favour of Temperance. The Earles- town and Newton United Bands of Hopi, held their demonstration on Saturday after- noon. The Warrington Band of Hope Union achieved a great success on Monday, With its precession of 3,500 persons, and Gala attended by ro,ooo. The teetotallers let it be seen that they can enjoy themselves Without intoxicating liquors, and in the light of day. There were singing, reciting, dancing, and races, followed by earnest and _effective speeches in support of the temperance cause. At Runcorn, proceed- ings were commenced on Sunday, when there Was a temperance meeting and a temperance sermon. On Monday, the Sons of Temper- lice gathered in gfeat force, and, attended oY bands and banners, formed themselves i into a procession, and proceeded to a field Where some 2.000 persons enjoyed them- selves to their hearts' content. In the even- ing, there WAS a tea meeting in Bethesda ssohoolroom which was largely attended. The ticretarY presented a report which confirms one , common experience that a Friendly s•-ta-cnltY based upon temperance principles s nPon the soundest foundation. It was -u stated that the average sickness for the year as 6% days per member, while the average t'n nOn-tcmperance societies was "from ii c`c' 12 days per member." The record as to i ;,eatlis was equally satisfactory, the mortal- :l•3' being under 7 per 1,000, as against " 12 '0 1.5 per 1,000 " where the total abstinence Was not enforced. These figures are certainly yery striking—not to say startling—as show- ing that, other things being equal, the per- son who joins a Temperance Friendly So- ac inedt ygrgeraetal yt 1 greatly nlcersesaesness hishi s chancesliability ot Of longevity as compared with the individual who becomes a Member of a non-temperance organisation. But it may be urged—and fairly urged—that the records of a single year of a single society do not furnish sufficient data for a general conclusion. Let us grant this and look a little further afield. Speaking a few months , ago at :he annual meeting of the Rugeley Temperance Union, the Earl of LICHFIELD, Who is a Rechabite, said : In three places—Blackburn, Bolton, and Manches- Ler—there were Rechabite Tents ivith 3,400 mem- -I"ers, and in Blackburn there were Oddfellows' i lodges with 3,500 members. In 1876 the number of deaths amongst the 3,400 Rechabites was 46, and he number Cif deaths amongst the Oddfellows was , 46, the difference being as between 13-5 and 21.53 ter I thousand. In ten years of the same experience we found that the deaths amongst the Rechabites as 13 in the thousand, as against 19 in the thou- rol amongst the Oddfellows. is surely something to "give us pause" that in a given period more Oddfellows by , 1 nne-half die as compared with Rechabites. It is not that Oddfellows intemperate or Weakly are as a body of men; but they have in- te InPerate men amongst them. They have, 1 ,o proportion of " moderationis 0, a ts,' ul 4.1_ t' who, to,i'ne end, become intemperate ; and the re- is seen in those brief statistical records rg: disease and death which tell a long story With are not to be gainsaid. It is the same Z.l‘ll sickness as with death; the advantages 1 aclo the side of the abstainer. " For five Yes,,,ne: the Earl of Lichfied says, "the sick- Per member amongst the Rechabites Z3` six days, and the payment per member sr:kBd ; while amongst the Oddfellows the Da, ness Per member was 17 days, and the tittneni Per member 26s 3,0." By comparing it B.e figures wi.h those of the Runcorn Society, Will b Of tk e seen that the sickness of the members Runcorn Sons of Temp ..tte , Temperance is an aver- th Qinongst Temperance Societies, and that erg is , by th no escaping the conclusion come to 104 e local secretary, namely, that with Qes:er life, they had less than half the sick- fa of non-temperance societies. In view of vr,ets of h' ...int t is kind, we cannot but urge upon , a ra•g 'men who are thinking ot providing ,or aboultlY day to consider well what they are t in They making choice of a Friendly Society. ' Sely May be strong and temperate them- ha es, but what of their fellows? They may ve to 4ble Carry others on their backs who are less to ordi_u resist temptation. Indeed, in the this wa.ry course of things, it is inevitable that tc,l_f ehr,l•ll be so, more or less, but it is a matter Qe nicTice in the first instance whether it shall llerall re or less. The Runcorn Sons of Tern- include a fair proportion of the tern- ittt—l—Ce men of the town, and their numbers wnstantly increasing. Still it is but a

proportion, and it is a proportion which should be largely increased. In Warrington the Rechabites are a flourishing body con- sidering their numbers, but their numbers are small considering the population. Bands of Hope are of incalculable service in training the young in the way they should go; they lay the foundation of many a good and useful life, but we cannot but think that those who conduct them might with propriety and ad- vantage urge "the older end" to tie them- selves to temperance by joining a Temperance Friendly Society. We know that these Bands of Hope are attached to various sects, and that there is such a thing as sectarian jealousy. But there is, or should be, no room for its exercise in this matter, for we are right, we believe, in saying that Temperance Friendly Societies exclude not only intoxica- ting liquors, but religious and political con- troversy. Under such a happy condition of things, it is not to be wondered at that the members of such institutions have less sick- ness and longer lives than fall to the lot of ordinary humanity. They ought, like TEN- NYSON'S brook, to "go on for ever."

It is high time that a Society for the Preservation of Ancient Footpaths was es- tablished for the Warrington district. From the evidence which has already been brought together, there can be no question that the footpath leading to Morley Corr Trion, which the Railway Company are attempting to close at the instigation of the agent of Sir GILBERT GREENALL. is an ancient right of way, and that as such it is the property of the public. From .a letter which we pub- lish in our present issue, it will be seen that this is not the only footpath in which the Walton baronet is interested, that has been closed to the public. The second path re- ferred to led from Appleton through the Denna to Hatton ; and it is apparent that, though the use of it can be traced back to two generations, the present generation is to be denied access to it, if they do not bestir I themselves and exercise their rights. We observe, too, that the Newton Commissioners are being called upon to open a footpath ' which is now closed, and which led across what is known as the Mesnes, near Earles- town. In this case, as in others, the people are being robbed to serve private ends; and it is the duty of public bodies which have authority in such matters to step in and secure the rights of the public But an im- pulse requires in the first instance to be rightly given and rightly direc- ted ; hence the need of some such organisation as a Footpaths Preservation Society. Besides, the knowledge of its ex- istence would be a terror to evil-doers. We are inclined to think that, if there had been a Footpaths Society in Warrington, Sir GIL- BERT GREENALL would not have permitted his agent to write to the Railway Company to induce them to close the road leading to Morley Common; he would probably have taken his chance for breeding snipe without interfering with the rights of men. If no other consideration had influenced him, he would have thought--" These footpath openers will make a fuss, and votes just now are of more value than snipe." But the mischief is done and requires to be undone. To this end a Society should be formed at once; and in aid of such a laudible undertaking, we shall be glad to receive the names of those I who are willing to beco ne members of a 'society. .Meantime we would advise people who have been in the habit of walking over the Morley Common footpath to continue to use it. Sir GILBERT GREENALL'S game- keeper may threaten, but he cannot prose- cute—his master is only tenant of the land. As for the Railway Company, we d 3 not be- lieve they would prosecute if they could. , They know their own interests too well to fly in the face of the public, to say nothing of putting their customers who live at Walton , and Daresbury to great inconvenence. With the battle half won, there must be no sur- render.

Since the above was written and put in type, we have, at the eleventh hour, received a letter on the subject of the Morley Com- mon footpath from Mr. HAMPSON, the Con- servative agent, and we make room for it, though at some inconvenience. He is ready to "re-affirm as absolutely correct" every- thing he has previously stated ; but we trust he will pardon us if we say that, in view of the facts which have been disclosed, something more is needed than his affirmation. If Sir GILBERT GREENALL is SO "sweetly innocent" as he would have people believe, the landlord of Walton must be very badly served by his gamekeeper and by his agent. And how is he relieved of responsibility, seeing that Mr. T. SMITH BURGESS has written to the Railway Company as "agent for Sir GILBERT GREENA.LL ? " Are we to understand that both agent and gamekeeper have been con- spiring to defraud the public of a right of way, and at the same time damage their master's chances at the next election? If so, what has Sir GILBERT done to bring them to book for their bad be- haviour ? It would be interesting to know, too, if he has written to the Railway Com- pany—this time in his own name—to say that hisa.,lgn such a ensthadn omatterbusiness ; a to writet a t, on nowhis be- half that his attention has been i cadlled to the stopped footpath across Sni bave wrongly ' gaetn e n Railway Company KenwPaiellant he desires that the reverse the action they instance of "T. GREENALL." Whilst he is in the way of 100 - SMITEHNABrIR„GEss, Sir GILBERT doingsa genfatsnt dhwbohsroie bring gmactehtd edwirleitmsho mas- ter look- ing into pt ehres and their master's authority, ter into disrepute, it will be as well if he will see to the Appleton footp tth which has also been improperly closed. We shall be glad to give Sir GILBERT GREENALL credit for all he does in the way of restoration.l He has a rare opportunity; but we must I have deeds, not words. With regard to Mr. Hampson's electoral delusions, we will leave him to be dealt with by the Liberal agent. Mr. ROBERTS has finished him off so neatly in the matter of the footpaths question that we are quite sure he will be equal to ex- posing the series of fictions to which Mr. HAMPSON has appended his name.

WHAT is known as the St. Helens poison- ing case was tried at the Liverpool assizes on Saturday, and it ended in the criminal, JOHN PEARSON, being sentenced to penal servitude for twenty years PEARSON is a labourer, 33 years of age. His wife died some time ago, and he was left in distressed circumstances with three children, the eldest of whom is nine years of age. Rather than face the prospect of their being taken to the work- house, he conceived the horrible idea of poisoning them, and with this object he ob- tained and administered a quantity of oxalic acid. He then went to the house of a neigh- bour and stated that he had poisoned the , children. Fortunately, the little ones, though

div.head: EXA.MTNER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 8. 1885.
div.p: THE EXA.MTNER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 8. 1885.

dangerously ill, were not dead, and emetics being given in time their lives were saved. The prisoner at his trial told the jury that he had given his children the oxalic acid in a mistake ; but a defence so utterly opposed to the facts of the case could not be accepted, for, apart from his having told a neighbour that he had poisoned the children, he had written a note requesting that they should let his brother at Burnley know, and conclud- ing—" only sorry they are not dead." If the poisoning had been an accident, he would have acted in a wholly different way, and used wholly different language. PEARSON deliberately tried to get rid of his children and, assuming that he was in his right mind when the terrible crime was committed, he deserves the heavy sentence which Mr. Justice MANISTY passed upon him. But was he in his right mind ? It is not unreasonable, it seems to us, to have a doubt on the point. In the first place, though he proceeded in so careful a manner to obtain and prepare the oxalic acid, he took no precaution to conceal his crime. On the contrary, he went out of his way to make it known. Then the reason giv,n for seeking to destroy the children, namely, that he did not want them to have to go to the Workhouse is suggestive of an unhinged mind rather than of a powerful motive, how- ever erroneous or bad. It is to be regretted that the Prisoner had not the benefit of counsel, who could have investigated the cir- cumstances of the case, and stated what was required to be itated on his behalf. There are people who are temporarily insane, and it may be that PEARSON is one of this class. If he really sought—fully conscious of what he was doing—to murder his children because they were a burden to him, he richly merits the crushing sentence which he is doomed to ' undergo.

WE present our readers this week with a map of the course of the projected Ship Canal between Manchester and Liverpool. It will, we do not doubt, be scanned with espe- cial interest now that the course the Canal will take may be said to be beyond con- troversy. The House of Commons Committee of Inquiry held its last sitting on Monday— Bank Holiday; on Wednesday the Bill passed its final stage in the House of Commons amid general cheers; and on Thursday the Royal assent was given in the House of Lords.

SWINE FEVER.—Tbe townships of Widnes and Dutton have been declared free from this disease which has, how- ever, broken out at Weston and Weston Point. Ilevrow PAROCHIAL TRIP.—The SI:10Ra Parochial trip of the Halton Parish Church took place yesterday, when tibqut 200 persons journeyed from Widnes Central Station to Southport. RUNCORN CO-OPRRATIVR Socurrv.—A dividend of 2s ed in the pound has been declared for the past half-year The net profits realised amounted to £4,174 Cs 6.1, and £lll 16s was drawn from the reserve laud to enable the dividend to be paid. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—An open air meeting was held at An- derson's-corner on "thursday evening, when a large audience was addressed by Mr. E. A. Parr, of Liverpool, on the evils of intemperance. The bancl was in attendance and escorted the members front and to the schoolroom. ROUNDERS MATCH AT RUNCORN.—On Saturday, the Beacom Y.M.C.A. played the Widnes White Star at Run- corn. In the first innings the T.M L.A. scored 34, and their opponents 29; but in the second the White Srar ran up a total of 91, and the Y.M.C.A. were all out for 24 rues. TREAT TO EMPLOYES AT RUNCORN.—Messrs. Boydell and Coventry, tailors, Church-street, Runcorn, gave their third annual treat to their employes on Monday. An enjoy- able day was spent at Llandudno, dinner bring provided at EVAOS' Temperance Hotel. The firm defrayed all ex. penses. • WIDNES PARLIAMENTARY DIVISIONS. Mr. Goff, the assistant overseer, has placed on the doors of all the places of worship in Widnes the new list of vc.tirs, dm. The number of persons qualified to vote in the town has in- creased from 800 to 4.300. All Liberals should me that their names are recorded. RUNCORN PARISH CEIURCH.—Tbe annual treat to the scholars attending the Parish Church Sunday School tOOls piece yesterday. To the number of about 900 they went to a field at Cavendish Farm, Weston, where swings, La-saws, football, and other means of enj iyment were provided. The Weston Church Band was in attendance. FLOWER SERVICE AT RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.—

T.Arge congregations ass4mbled in the Parish Church on Sunday' afternoon and evening, when offerings of flowers were received for the Cnester and Liverpool infirmaries. The cheir,aided by several female voices,teodered selections of classical music in good style. The preachers were the Rev. R. Edwards,,,f Newtown Mission, and he Rev. G. H. Staire, of Birkenhead. The collections, in aid of the choir treat, amounted to LIO. SAMARITAN LODOE 1.0.G.T., WIDNES.—AL the weekly meeting of the memners of this lodge, on Monday evening, Bro J. Jones, W.C.T., presided, and there was a good at tendance. The chief business of the evening was he eke. Hon of officers for the ensuing year. ,Bro. T. S. Machin, et Runcorn, was appointed W.C.T., and the following officers were also constituted :—Bros. Tomlinson, W.O , Hewson, W.F.S.; G. Widders, W.M. ; J. Widders, W I G. ; Coombs, MS. ; Sister Webb, W.T. ; Sister Lamb, W.D.M. BANE HOLIDAY AT RUNCORN.—AII the shops were c'osed on Bank Holiday, but with the exception of Camden Soso Works all the other works were in full swing. The rail way _ . .

traffic was very heavy, special trains being run to Frodsham. Nine hundred passengers booked for this pretty spot. Cheater and Liverpool was the destination of a considerable number. The demonstration of the Sans of Temperance proved an attraction to those who stayed at home. THE 2ND C.R.V.—These volunteers have during the past week been camping out at Southport. Tne F and 11. (Runcorn) Companies departed on Saturday under the command of Captain C. W. Haziehurst, Captain Joliffe, and Lieutenants Rhodes, Joule, and Timmins. There were about 108 rank and file; but this number has been increased during the week. The total number in camo has been Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton, 6 captains, 11 lieutenants, 610 men, 2 majors, 2 minlstere, and 1 doctor; total, 623. The annual inspection took pl ice yesterday. SERIOUS CHARGES AGAINST A FARMER.—On Thursday afternoon, Henry Beard, farmer, of Upton Rock, was charged at the Whines Police Court with stealing two horses, value £l3O, from fields at Ditton and Crouton, on Monday night. Police-constable Thompson deposed to re- ceiving the prisoner and the horses into custody at Doncas- ter, and on the way hack the prisoner said he booked the horses at Warrington and received them at Doncaster. He denied that hti had stolen them. The prisoner was re- manded until Tuesday next. The court was full of farmers. TRESPASSING ON THE RAILWAY AT BUNCO/VC—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, George Dennis, a dock labsurer, of 7, Cartwright-street. Halton-road, was charged with tres- passing upon the London and North*Western Railway at Sutton.—Mr. C. Ferrand, of the solicitors' department, Liverpool, prosecuted.—John Wright, detective. of Bt. Helens, deposed to seeing the defendant upon the lines at Sutton near a place where notice boards were displayed warning against trespassing.—Tbe defendant said he was searching for some young throstles.—The Bench imposed a i fine of 5s and costs.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held yesterday at the Town Hall, Watorloo-road, Runcorn, under the presidency of Mr. J. Pritchard Present—Messrs T. Norman, R. Lea. and F. Rigby (clerk). The deed for the transfer of the land forming the site of the new Board schools in Greenway-road, for the Runcorn Property and Investment Company, was signed and sealed. The Clerk of the Works reported that the erection of the echoOlt.‘ was preceding in a satisfactory manner.—Mr. Norman re, marked that the buildings would be completed in Novem- ber, but he did not think it would he WiSe to Open them until after Christmas. There was no other busineee. ANNUAL FESTIVAL OF FEODSDAm BECHABITES. The annual festival of the Delight of Frodsham Tent. No 230, of Independent Order of Rechabites, was held at Frodsham on Bank Holiday, when the members walked in procession through the town, headed by the Frodsham Parish Church Bible Class Brass Band. After visiting their patron*, a public tea was partaken of in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom' and an adjournment afterwards took place to the Church field, kindly lent for the occtsion by Mr. Peter Warburton. From the annual statement of accounts pre- pared by the secretary (Mr. W. Lockett), it appears that the number of members is 86, and the SUM of £77 19i had been distributed to sick members during the year, and £22 for funerals. The total fund of the Tent at the close of the year was £233 ds 7d. RUNCORN FERN LIBRARY.—The monthly meeting was held in the Commissioners' Board-room, on Wednesday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. W. Handley. Mr. J. D. Jones, the librarian, reported that during the month of July there were 1.080 volumes borrowed from the lending department, and 30 from the reference department; total, 1,110, an increase of 62 on the corresponding month last year. It was resolved that the Dictionary of National Biography now publishing, and to be completed in 50 vols. at 12e 6d each, be obtained for the reference department of the Library. The secretary was instructed to apnly to the Commissioners for the transfer of a sum of £5O to the Library account. Accounts amounting to £ll 5s 7d for books were passed for payment. Daring the month volumes had been presented by the executors of the late Mrs. Steele,' by Dr. Steele ; by Mr. W. F. Blake, Mr. .J. Simpson, and Dr. A. C. Fryer (author), of Bristol. SHOCKING BRUTALITY &T WlDNE9.—Before Mr. H. Gas- kell, jun., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, .John Fox, a labourer, living at 19, Viaduct-street, was charged en re- mand with committing a rape upon Martha Johnson, 11 years of age, who resides with her parents at 17, Viaduct street. Mr. Knowles defended. About eight o'clock on Saturday, the 25th ult., the girl was left in the house alone by her mother. During her absence the prisoner carried 1 the girl into his own house and committed the assault upon the bed. He was discovered by his wife who called him a brute. The screams of the girl and her shouts of "murder, murder," and " mother, mother," were heard in the street by neighbours, who came to the conclusion that the girl was being thrashed. When apprehended by P.C. Evans, the prisoner said " I expected you I thought of running away and then I thought I had better face it out. The girl asked me for sixpence." Later he said " But for the drink I should not have done it."—Dr. McLennan deposed to the Injuries sustained by the girl, and the prisoner was corn- mitted to the Liverpool Assizes for trial.

A WIDNES TRADESMAN CONVICTED OF TURFY. —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. H. Gaskell- William Proctor, manager of a butcher's shop in Waterloo, road, for Mr. T. Lawrinson, was lerought up on remand charged with stealing 21bs of paint, value is, the property of James Wilson, painter, 54, Irwell-street, Widnes. The particulars of the case were leported in last Saturday's issue.—Mr. J. W. Knowles defended, and contend( d that it WAS merely a practical joke, and that there was no felonous intent in taking the paint. He was a young man about to be married and start in business on his own account. Up to the present time he had borne an unblemished char icter. and he was sure their worships must feel that it would be a great hardship to tarnish his reputation by a conviction in a case like this. He commented upon the fact that the paint was taken openly, and concluded by an appeal for the prisoner's discharge.—Mr. Gaskell said the Bench were of opinion the prisoner did steal the paint, and that it was all very well to say it was a practical joke after proceedings were taken. A fine of 103, or, in default, 14 days, was im- posed. ACTION AGAINST A WIDNES GENTLEMAN.—At the Liver- pool Assizes, on Monday, an action was heard before Mr. Justice Lopes and a special jury in which Mr. Josiah Wycliff Kynaston, stated to be a gentleman of some con- siderable distinction as a chemist, sought to recover from Major James Cross, of Widnes, a large sum as damages for alleged breach of agreement. The plaintiff was repro!. sented by Mr. Gully, Q.O , and Mr. Taylor. and Mr. Rus- sell, Q.C., M.P., was the leading counsel for the defendant. It was stated that plaintiff had lately been in the employ of Messrs. Chadwick an Sons, and had managed for them a large chemical works at St. Helens. Whilst there he had invented and patented several improved chemical processes ' In which it appeared Messrs. Chadwick claimed an interest, but some difference arising Major Cross was called in as an arbitrator. Ultimately Major Cross made overtures t ) the plaintiff which induced the latter to offer Messrs Chadwick, a sum of money for their interest in the patents, and arrange- ments were made by which Major Cross was to finance the plaintiff with a view to worsing out the patents in a jaint partnership between them. The present action was brought npoe this alleged agreement, which the defendant new denied having entered into. The plaintiff further alleged part performance of the agreement, insomuch as several contracts for the simply of chemicals, chiefly of a luminous c eke, were entered into by the plaintiff in the interest of the firro with the authority of the defendant. A large num- ber of letters were put in, and his lordship said the question in the action was as to tbe construction to be placed upon the correspondence, but he thought it was a matt-r which ought to be referred. The parties thereul. on, at the sugges- tion of the learned judge, agreed ts a nominal verdict for L the plaintiff, subject to the reference.

RUNCORN POLICE NEWS —OR Thursday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. James Handley, Agnes Constantine,a tramp, was sentenced to seven days hard labour for being drunk in Halton-road, on the previous day. and to a further term of seven days for begging in High•street. The former Case was proved by P.S. Neild and the second by Mrs. Eliztbeth Unsworth. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS —The fortnightly meet- ing was held on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. Had- field. Present —the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Hewitt, Speakman, Norman, T. Lewis. Wallington, Aaron. Nrild, H. Linaker (clerk). and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). The only matter of interest was a letter from Dr. Weaver to the Guardians for the increase of salary they had grantel to him.

TEES REPRESENTATION' OF MONTROBB.—At a meet- ing of representatives of the Montrose Burghs, held on Wednesday, Dr. Mackie, of Warrington' who was present, was unanimously adopted as the Conserva- tive candidate, and agreed at once to address the burghs. NEw CourrrY MAGISTRATES.—The following gen- tlemen have been placed on the Commission of Peace for Lancashire :—Mr. John Hargreaves, Bacup Mr. J. Hargreaves Bolton, Newchurch, Rossendale ; and Mr. Robert Handsley, and Mr. Thomas Mason, both of Colne.

PENKETH LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—On Saturday 'afternoon the members of the above association had their annual trip. The place selected was Tabley Old Hall. By the kindness of Lord de Tabley a ticket of admission was given to inspect the grounds, the Hall, and. chapel. The party to the number of about 60 left the Liberal Club at 1-15, going through Warrington, Latchford. and High Leigh, arriving there about 3-15. A minute inspec- tion was made of the Hall, grounds, and chapel. The return journey was resumed at 8-15, arriving back at Penketh about 10-45.

Tins Inorr TRADE.—An important report has I been issued by the Iron Trades Employers' Associa- tion. It deals with the depression in trade, and mentions that a special inquiry made by the Association has elicited over 700 returns, represent- ing a direct employment in the engineering, mould- ing, steam boiler making, and iron ship building , branches of upwards of 118,000 hands. Trade is declared "good" in regard to 2,500 of these per- sons, " moderate " as to 25,000, and "bad" or "very bad" in respect to the remaining 90,500. The con- dition of trade, it is remarked, shown by these returns seems not unlikely to influence the wages question unless some improvement comes to the aid , of the employers at an early date. A 50 YEAR-OLD RELIC.—An Earlestown corre- spondent writes :—What might be termed a" 50 years' relic " is to be observed in the brick wall on the left-hand side of the road to the Vulcan, about 200 yards from the foundry, and just at the turn of the road. The relic is an iron plate some 4 feet 6 inches in length, and the undermentioned inscrip- tion which it bears is in iron letters. Considering that the " tablet° is exactly 50 years of age this year, it has well stood the storms and other atmos- pherical disturbances of the last half century. The inscription is as follows :—" Take notice. Y'rivate property. We do hereby caution all hawkers, rag I and bone dealers, beggars, ballad singers, &c., from trespassing on these premises. Any person or, per- sons of the above description found hereon after this notice will be prosecuted with the utmost rigor of the law. Vulcan Foundry, May Ist, 1835." MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—The weekly meet- ing of the Provisional Committee was held in the Boardroom, Manchester, on Friday afternoon, Mr. William Fletcher presiding. The statement of ac- counts brought down to the 31st July, which had been duly examined and certified to be correct by the auditors, was laid upon the table. It was re- ported that Mr. Adamson. accompanied by Alderman Husband, Mr. Henry Boddington, Junr., Mr. Leader Williams, Mr. Saxon, and other gentlemen had, on the 6th inst., paid a visit of inspection to the Til- bury Docks, on the river Thames, now in course of construction.- The works consist of a large tidal basin and dock, to a great extent on a similar plan to the proposed Manchester and Salford docks, just sanctioned by Act of Parliament. Nearly 5,000 men are employed upon the works, and 280 locomotives, steam navies, pumping engines, and other machines, all worked by steam. The wages paid amount to £7,300 per week. The deputation were much pleased with their visit as they saw how easily and rapidly such a great engineering work was being carried out under conditions much less favourable than the proposed ship canal works. CHESHIRE FARMER'S AND THE GENERAL ELEC- norr.—A special general meeting of the Chester I Farmers' Club was held at Chester, on Saturday, to I discuss certain questions which it is' proposed to put to Parliamentary candidates at the General If4leetton, The queAtions submitted had been adopted by committees of the Wirral, Warrington. Wigan, and Chester Farmers' Clubs. Ultimately the meet- ing, by a majority, decided that candidates should be asked whether they would vote (1) for the main roads of the county to be maintained out of the im- perial fund; (2) for the election of county govern. ment boards; (3) for an amendment of the Agri- cultural Holdings Act, so that the sitting tenant should be protected from having his rent raised on his own improvements; (4) for compelling railway companies to charge for the carriage of farm pro- duce rates which do not exceed those charged for the carriage of the goods of other industries; (5) greater freedom for cultivation and absolute cer- tainty of compensation for unexhausted improve- ments; (6) equalisation of local rates; (7) the pre- Bent regulations excluding stock from infected coun- tries; (8) the abolition of tithes; (9) and the support lof all these measures if brought forward by either political party. AN INTERRUPTED COURTSIIIP.—P.S. Commias, stationed at Newton, is the owner of" a clever dog," which has gained notoriety by its detection of per- sons who, in various ways, have been committing offences against the laws of the country. It is known as the "dog detective," and its captures have been several times reported. Another incident in its career occurred late on the night of Saturday last. PS. Commins was on duty near the Vulcan, Earlestown, and when passing a field of oats be- longing to Mrs. Ann Wright, the dog rushed into the field and began to bark furiously. The officer un- derstood this as an intimation that everything must not be right, and he thereupon entered the Held. He made the discovery that "lovers twain " —a young woman residing at the Vulcan, and her admirer from the neighbourhood of Vitriol-square, had in the exuberance of their emotion trespassed into the " sweet solitude" of the oat field. The un- expected appearance of P.S. Commins was an un- welcome surprise to the happy pair. The sequel will transpire, it is believed; in proceedings before a bench of magistrates. The police constable who served the summonses was informed by the gushing Juliet that she would not have been receiving that (meaning the summons) if it had not been for "that there dog." Loving as she is, she has no affection for the dog.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

THE BLOCKING OF WEST BANN-STREET, WIDITES.—The difficulty in regard to this matter is in a fair way towards settlement. Messrs. Bolton and Son have accepted the sug- gestions made by the Local Board, &nd at the meeting on Tuesday next an agreement for the closing of the street will probably be submitted for approval. It is expected that employment will be given to a large number of persons by the extension of Messrs. Bolton's works.

A CORONER'S JURY AT VARIANCE —Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, on Saturday resumed the inquest upon Peter Walton, a labourer, 63 years of age, who committed suicide in his own house at Farnwortb on the 24th ult. On the previous occasion the jury were unable to agree upon a verdict, and the. inquiry was adjourned. The jury, after a short consultation together, returned a verdict to tbe effect that the deceased committed suicide whilst temporarily insane.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES VOLUNTEERS AT ALTCLR.-At the prize meeting of the Cheshire Rifle Association at Alt- car, several prizes were won by the members of the F. (Run- corn) Company of the lad CRY. The priza of £lO in the first stage of the Lord Lieutenant's prize was won by Lieu- tenant Timmins, who scored 94 points. Sergeant W. H. Harvey with 88 points took a prize of £l. In the Sweet- hearts' CompAition. Lieutenant Timmins and Sergeant Harvey each scored 31 points each, winning M. Sergeant G. Junor, of the 21st L R.V., Widnes, scored 32 points and secured a prize of a like sum. In the aggregate prizes, 88 points were scored by Sergeant Dwerrybouse, who won £l.

-- ANOTHER SEWER ACClngtgr i WlDNES.—Another acci- dent occurred at the main sewer on Messrs. Hutchinson's estate, near Messrs Golding Davies and Company's works, on Tuesday. Mr. Randle, of the firm of contractors who are making the sewer, was sitting upon a projection in the excavation superintending the removal of a plank, when he was overcome by the gas and would have fallen hut for tt e promptitude of a workman. Ile was brought to the surface in a semi-unconscious condition, and after the application of the usual remedies recovercd. It will be remembered that Mr. Randles had a very narrow escape of meeting his death through a plucky attempt to save A servant, who had be- come "gassed." CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WESTON POINT. Upon the exposed position of Westrin Point Pier a meeting in sup- port of the candidature of Mr. W. H. Verdin, the Conserva- tive candidate for the Northwich division. was held on Tuesday evening. The audience was composed mainly of supporters of the party from Runcorn, a few voters from the immediate neighbourhood, and a large number of boys, whose conduct was somewhat boisterous—On the motion of Mr. J. J. Speakman, the Rev. J. J. Bryant, incumbent of the parish, was voted to the chair.—Mr. Verdin addressed the meeting as a moderate Conservative and as a representa- tive of the salt trade.—On the motion of Mr. Z. Rozenberg, seconded by Captain Whitfield, and supported by Mr. Cope, a resolutlon to support Mr. Verdin was passed, the chair- man thinking it necessary to tell the boys present not to vote.

I —H—LT" I/MARIE'S AT RuNcontr.—Within the past few weeks 11 several burglaries, happily not of a very serious character, have taken place, and the police have been keeping a sharp look out. At an early hour on Sunday morning the resi- dence of Mr. F. A. Lake, solicitor, in Greenway-road, was entered at the back, and several lbs. of beef and some butter was taken. In the same neighbourhood several young ducks were purloined, and an attempt was also made to enter the house of Mr. Peter Wright, Greenwav-road. About six o'clock Mr. Wright heard a noise in the kitchen, and, descending the stairs, was somewhat startled to find a man with his body half way through the open window. The man rapidly made his exit, and Mr. Wright entered upon an unsuccessful pursuit. He was, however, able to identify the man, who was subsequently apprehended by P.C. Ham- mersley. The prisoner, who is a loafer named Peter Lowe, was brought before the magistrates on Thursday, and re- manded until Tuesday. It was stated that he had thrown three keys into the canal, and than threatened that if taken into custody he would make somebody pay for H. HANK HOLIDAY AT WIDNES.-510tIday last was obser- Yea as a holiday by the tradesmen of the town, but the chlmnies of the chemical mannfacturies indicated the fact that operations were going briskly forward as on other days. Many of the employ6a had, however, got leave of 'absence, and the trains for Lancashire watering places. Hale, Overton Hills, drc., were well filled. In the morning the local branch of the Order of Foresters had a demon- stration. Attired in their bright regalia and headed by a banner and the Soap Works Brass Band, about 50 members paraded the main thoroughfares in the presence of a large number of spectators. In the afternoon the Parish Church Bible Class had their annual trip. To the number of about 60, they journeyed to Newton Lake, being accompanied by Mr. F. H. Pankhurst, president of the class, the Rev. .1. Wright Williams, and the Rev. C. Rumfitt. A very enjoy- able time was spent, a good tea was provided by Mrs Bray. During the afternoon a presentation took place to Mr. Pankhurst, who is about to sever his connection with the class consequent upon changing his residence. On behalf of the members Mr. Brooks handed him a very beautiful edition of the revised version of the Bible as a token of the esteem and respect in which he is held. In ackowledging the gift Mr. Pankhurst said they were not to suppose that his labours sea teacher amongst them were in any way re- laxing, for whenever opportunity offered he ihould be pleased to give them his best services. cACALllhidiaaßornradelaeumfieuknres tl c ordrl Wallington, aentt wl tin the (deputy ußhg tett: ryoci che,:LeNi rr ke) nightly meeting was held on Tuesday. div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday. Present— Messrs. R. Shaw (chairman), Norman Dobson, Williams, Grine, Speakman, Lake, Taylor, Meadowcroft, Lightburn, Fisher, Pritchard. White, Whittaker, Harris, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), :‘,larshall (ecretary), and Barker (sur- veyor).

div.head: TEE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: TEE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

Dr. .1. W. Mouritz, brother of the late medical officer, re. ported that daring the past month there were 20 deaths registered in Runcorn. The death rate was 15 per 1,000 per annum. The health of the town was at present satis- factory, and the rate of mortality low.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the Highway Committee contained a reso- lution that the line if the proposed Salvation Army Bar- racks, in Bigh-street, be the same as that of Bank Cham- bers. It was recommended that a medical officer be appointed at a salary of LIO per annum.—ln moving the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Meadowcrcfc said there was a small increase suggested in the salary of the medical officer, but the duties were rusch heavier than when the original salary was fixed—Mr. Norman seconded the motion, which was carried.

div.head: MARKET.
div.p: THE MARKET.

The Market Superintendent reported that the receipts for the past month amounted to £26 2a 4d, an increase of £2 8s 5d on the corresponding month last year. It was recom- mended that Messrs. Joseph Kirkham and Co's. tender for repairing the roof of the Market Hall for the sum of £63 58 be accepted.—The minutes were adopted, on the motion of Mr. Dobson, seconded by Mr. Norman.

div.head: HEAVY SURCHARGES -THE AUDITOR CRITICISED
div.p: HEAVY SURCHARGES -THE AUDITOR CRITICISED

The Finance Committee reported thst the district auditor had disallowed £7O and £144 Os 4J law costs, charges, and expenses incurred by the Commissioners in an opposition in Parliament to the passing of the Manchester Ship Canal Rill, also £65 7s 6.1 expenses in connection with that opposi- tion. He also disallowed £7 106 charged as the cost of re- pairing and removing a clock, and £270, the balance of an untaxed bill of costs in the case of Thomas Beesley v. the Runcorn Commissioners. The auditor said with regard to the sums of £214 Os 4d and £65 7s 6cl that the expenses of opposing the bill were not authorised, taxed, examined, and allowed as required by law ; with regard to the sum of £73 14e 2d, part of the slim of £214 Os 4d, there were no particulars or vouchers for payment of the expenses included in that sum submitted to the Commis- sioners or to him at the audit and such sum was excessive lw the sum of £10; that as to the sum of £7 10s paid to Ihomas Pritchard, the Commissioners did not by resolution or otherwise legally authorise such expenditure, and there was no accepted tender for the same; neither were any particulars of the time occupied, or the materials used, in

the repairing and removing of the clock supplied to the Commissioners, or to him; that with regard to the sum of £270, the hill of costs of which this forms a part was not taxed or allowed by any conipetent authority; that tbe aforesaid sums of £214 Os 4d, .£7 lOs Ott, and £270 respectively, were paid .erici charged upon the funds of the Commissioners without lawful authority. —Mr. Fisher moved the confiruagtim of the minutes.—The Chairman, referring to the surcharges, said it was clear that the auditor had only now found out the proper way of tax- ing these bills of costs. A short time ago the Local Govern- , ment Board informed the Commissioners how these hills were to be taxed, and the auditor in the surcharges for the previous year was not aware of the method, because be did not give the same reasons. There was one thing in the reasons that seemed absurd. The auditor said that with regard to the item of £73 14s 2d he had no particulars or vouchers put before him ; that he had no means of knowing whether the e xptmditure was reasonahle or not. Now how could be say it was £lO more than it ought to have been ? (A laugh.) They would ask Mr. Dolby. through the Local Government Board, for an explanatioo.—Mr. Meadowcroft said Mr. Dolby was only discharging his duty in making these surcharges in connection with the ship eanal, inasmuch as the Board bad not cempli.d with the Borough Funds Act. They should have some fur Vier expl ,n aion with re- gard to the £73. It might be that although he had no documentary evidence he had some otb,,r information for his guidance, and they must mrt vet 13,.5s judgment —The minutes were passed.

TH./S.:MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL COSTS. It was resolved that the Parliamentary and Legal Com- mittee be authorised to take step; for the taxation of Mr. . H Linekere bill of costs and expenses of the depots- ion relative to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. THE FORTHCOMING ELEC lON A committee consisting of Messrs. Fisher, Speakman, and Lake was appoin.ed for the purpose of furnishing the r .turning officer with voting papers, etc., for the forth- coming election of Commissioners. THE MEDICAL OFFICEBSIIIP. Dr. MacDertgall was appointed medicel officer of health at a salary of £4O a year. THE ALLEGED SLANDER AGAINST THE CHAIRMAN. The Chairman (Mr. R. Shew) said there was a matter which required a little explanation. They were aware that the conduct of some members of the Board had been re- cently discussed, but all the facts were not quite brought to the front. One point that ought to be made clear was with reference to the £l2. It was shown be the books and documents produced at the Chester Assizes that the £l2 as I well as the £l4 had been clearly taken off the accounts. The matter did not rest entirely on any bare es parte state- merit. He wanted the Board to understand that it was not ; Mr. Linaker's law lull that was reduced. Owing to instruc- tions given by Mr. Linaker to the hotel proprietor, tee mem- bers staying at the hotel had not been able to receive sepa- rate accounts. The whole of the expenses were put down to Mr. Linaker. They would be aware that Mr. Lies- ker's costs, charges, and hotel expensas were put down in his law bill by that arrangement. He bad all the expenses put down in his name, and his share of the expenses were pet crown in the bill of the deputation. Mr. Linaker said he would willingly take off £l2, about his fair proportion of the hotel charges, leaving £3 19s 81 for incidental expenses in the bill of £73 14, 21, which they said nothing about. It was not a concession made by Mr. Linaker to the ratepayers, but they simply pre- vented him receiving twice over his hotel ex- peoses. The Law Clerk said this was a very serious charge to make against him, and be asked fora committee to inquire into the circumstances.— The Chairman said that Mr. Linaker's law bill contained, and should contain, all to which he was entitled, and if his hotel bill was in any other shape it had no business to come in his charges and costs of the deputation.—The Law Clerk: Did the £l2 that really came off go to the treasurer of the Commissioners 7—The Chairmen : It waa never paid at all. —The Law Clerk : Oh ! I can prove that in a very few minutes.—The Chairman : Here is the bill, which will prove that it never was drawn.—The LAW rk I hold a receipt from Mr. Pritchard for the mooey, that will prove whether it was drawn.—The Chairman : Mr. Linaker has put it on this bill—here it is in his own hand writing.—The Law Clerk : It is not my writing. It is the handwriting of my brother.—The Chairman then entered into a number of statisties.—The Law Clerk said that he held, that they should charge ten shilling a day for expenses.— The Chairman : You told the Board some minutes ago that you charged three guineas a day.—The Law Clerk: I said every day I represented some other Authority I charged you at three guineas per day, Slat when I was on your business only I charged you five guineas —The Chairman The hotel bill was £3B 4s 2d, and the expenses £47 10s, making £B5 14s 21 ; but the amount drawn by Mr Linaker from the Committee was 478 lea 21. There is the £l2. It was never drawn.—The Lew Clerk said that he stuck to his ten shillings a day in his bill of casts, and received it.— The Chairmae observed that the figures of the law e'er k provod that he was £l2 short of what would paw for the toll hotel bill.—Mr Lake said it appeared that the question at issue was whether the law clerk gave the deputation £l2 in bard cash. According to the figures as he (Mr. Lake) now read them the law clerk received £l2 short The Chairman : Yes, that is, the Commissioners drew £l2 less—The LAVr Clerk : Yes' I took £l2 tram the bill in my office and gave it over to Mr. Pritchard. The chair- man has distinctly stated that I was attempting to obtain my hotel expenses twice over.—Mr. Pritchard said he and Mr. Shaw asked Mr. Linaker to take something off the ex• rerri s of £B5 148 2d, as the committee had decided to re- duce their expenses by £l4 8s IL Mr. Linaker said "As have done very well out of this matter I agree to fake £l2 off " and he substituted the figures £73 14s 21 instead of £B5 14s 2d. It was then he. took the £l2 off and in that form. The Law Clerk: Why should I give the ratepayers of Run- corn the benefit of £l2? I was not bound to do it.—The Chairman; You didn't.—The Lew Clerk: I say I did. (Dis- order.)—The Chairman: Just allow Mr. Pritchard to finish. —Mr. Pritchard: The fact has been stated that we have had £l2. and we have divided His amongst ue. Where is it, then 7—The Law Clerk: I have explained where it is.—Mr. Norman: The money newer was drawn, so that it could not have been paid.—Mr. Pritchard: The £l2 was never han- dled by the membe.s of the deputation, mid we is no way benefited by it —The Law Clerk: You made up the differ. ence,,t)etween the 10s and 5s per day.—Mr. Lake said it was important that they should have a committee to investigate the whole question. If the charge had been a mite. taken one through a mixing up of figures, the proper apologies would be tendered. However, that was a matter for the committee to investigate.— Mr Grice thought that the whole matter had been settled in a court of justice.—The Law Clerk: But the Chairman has deliberately stated that I tried to get my hotel bill in L9O. don mixed- up with his hotel bill, and that I have also charged my kill in my bill of costs.—Mr Pritchard: We resign if we are guilty, and he resigns if be is.—The Chairman said, as the Law Clerk had mad, a statement, there was one word that he wished to say. Do not let it go forth that that was to be mixed up with whether the bill of Mr Linaker did contain his hotel expenses or not.—The Law Clerk: It is part of the question.—The Chairman : It is not part of the question at all. The state- ment hitherto has been clear that we have bad this money.. Let the investigation cover that.--e' Mr. Spealatfan thought that the case lead been settled by one of the most important arbitrators, Mr- Justice Stephens.' Ti's course now suggested would only lead to acrimony.— Mr. Lake proposed that Messrs. Fisher, Meadowcroft, Light- burn, and Harris be formed a committee to make each in- quiries and take such evidence as they'may think fit on the allegations that Messrs. Seaw, Pritchard, and Speakman re- ceived £l2. The name of Mr. Lake was added, and the mo- tion passed.—The Law Clerk remarked that his position was in the hands of the Board whatever the result of the inquiry was.—The meeting then terminated.

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION,
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION,
RUNCORN.

The 18th annual demonstration of the Runcorn branch of this order took place on Sunday and Monday last. On the afternoon of the former day a large number of the members gathered in Devonshire-square, whera a meeting was con- ducted by Mr. John Withington, the Grand Worthy Patri- arch. Addresses were delivered by Messrs. P. Pendlebury, J. W. Boyle, and L. M. Temperley. A procession was then formed to Bethesda Congregational Chapel, where the Rev. T. Hackett preached a sermon from the text "And every man that striyeth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a con uptible crown, but we an in- corruptible,"

Oa Monday afternoon the annual processton took place. Fortunately in spite of the lowering clouds and a cold wind, the weather was fine, and the success of the demon- stration was equal to if it did not surpass previous years, hundreds of persons gathering in the streets to witness this the chief event of Bank Holiday. The procession left Devonshire-square shortly after two o'clock. At the head rode three mounted marshals: Brothers T. Heesora, P.G.W.P,; J. Withington, G.W.P. ; and J. Jones, G.T. Then marched the Mill-brow Brass Band, followed by the beautiful banner of the Life Boat Crew Division. Twenty members of the branch of the Daughters of Temperance, amongst whom was Miss Howarth, of Manchester, Grand Presiding Sister, the charter being borne by Mrs Boyle and Miss Minnie Davies. The male members followed, their charter being held by Brothers T. J. Holt and 8. Tomlin- son. Camden Wesleyau Brass Bend headed the cadet sec• lion, which numbered nearly 100 members, the char- ter being borne by Brothers Hedley, Powell, and John H. Tickle. The rear of the procession, which was gay with flags and banners, and the strains of music, was brought up by the lifeboat, drawn on a wagon kindly lent and harnessed by Mr. John Moore, of Suther- land-street. The boat was captained by Mr. John Faulkner, who had for his crew, all attired in man-of-war costume, Brothers T. Wilson, S. Faulkner, W. Faulkner, and E. blob- son. The other boys in the boat were Masters Willie Cooks, J Bisbrovvn, George Jones, H. Edwards, W. Faulkner, J. Ellison, and W.4effrey. The boat was lent by Mr. Hulse, of Widnes. The total number in the procession was 300, and amongst those taking part may be mentioned Brothers W. Wightman, of London, Most Worthy Patriarch of Great Britain; W. H. Lowe, Grand Scribe of Manchester ; Rev. T. Hackett and T. Cooke, Grand Scribe of Cheshire. En route the procession stopped at the aesidences of Bros. A. Kemal], W.P., T„ Cooke, Dr. Robinson, S. M. Temper- ley, and the Rev. T. Hackett. Upon reaching Halton-road the procession diverged along Heath-road to a field kindly lent by Mrs. C. Hazieburst, and here an enjoyable after

none was spent by about 2000, people. The marshals were Brothers W. Heatherington, D. leisbrown, R Thomas, S. M. Temperley, J. W. Boyle, S. Henderson, and A. Goedier. TEA MEETING. In the evening a tea meeting WAB held in Bethesda School- room, and there was a large attendance. The tables were attended to by Mrs. Heesom, Mrs. Heatherington, Mrs. Cooke, Mrs. Gibson, Mrs. /3isbrown, Mrs. F. Cooke, Mrs. Handles, Miss Ellen Chadwick, Miss Elizabeth Chadwick, Miss Howarth, Miss Hibbert, Miisii ss EMamssiedym, gaftuisus, A. Jones, Mips Miss Knight, Miss H. Davies, m Pesk, Miss E. Bindles. and Miss Dames. Submquently the proceedings were thrown open to the public, and the chair was occupied by Mr. F. J Norman. Upon the platform were the keys. Thomas Hackett and W. Vanse, Mr. lie Wightman, Mos Howarth, Mess's. W. H. Lowe, J. Faulkner, J Jones, S. Tomlinson, W. Heatherington, W. Ince, T. J. Hole M. Jones, Joe. Wallington, D. Bisorown, R. Thomas, T. Heesom, S. M. Temperley, S. Henderson, and T. Cooke. At the outset the chairman presented two volumes to Masters .W. Cooke and H. Powell, for having during the past year succeeded in obtaining the highest number of membern for the cadet section. Mr. T. COOKE, Grand Scribe, said the report he had to make presented an encouraging picture of the Year's pro- ress. Their demonstration that day bad been a grand success, and he trusted their meeting would so inspire and stimulate them that they would one and all go forth with their minds made up to fight and not to rest until every victim of the drink-curse was delivered and the country knew the clink-shop no more. That was one of the great objects of their society; in fact. all their forms and cere- monies directed the attention of their members to the great need of the day—the redemption of Britain from the curse of drink. The orderwas the ark of safety to which many a poor drunkard had taken shelter, given him happiness, where before there was nothing but Dv/item, and in addition mak- ing him a good citizen, and above all makieg him a better father and a better husband. The progress of the order during the year had been very satisfactory. Twentmfive new lodges had been constituted, besid.a 11 cadet sections, tbe number of divisions now being 397, end the number of cadet sections 107. In their merneership they had a net increese of 1,552, and in their funds an increase of £5,270 2s 61, their total membership now being 20.743, and the amount of their funds £62,662 16a Bd. During the year the order had paid in sick claims £14,398 19s 4d ; in death claims £2,642 55, and given away to mem- bers in distress £272 10s 4d. In their own division their membership had increased to 243, and the number of cadets to 100. The juveniles were increasing week by week under the superintendence of Bro. S. Henderson. During the year the division lead paid in sick claims £209 7s 34, and in death claims £.34. Besides this, £37 lOs had ben paid into the district central fund, in addition to what th-y had been able to retain in the hands of the treasurer, £49 ss. In order to explain this, he had to say that their funds were centrelieed in a central fund, to which the whole of their quarterly receipts were sent, with the exception of 3s per member, which was reserved to mast the working expenses of the division. The sickness amongst the members of the order during the year had averaged oi days per member, while in non-temperance societies the sickness had avereged from 11 to 12 days per member. The death rate in the Sons of Temperance Order had been a little under 7 per thousand, while in the non-temperance orders the percent ege of deaths had been from 12 to 15 per thousand, so that they saw they had a longer life with half the sickness which non-temper- ance societies had. Having further alluded to the advant- ages of the order, Mr. Cooke earnestly invited all young men to join their ranks. (Applause.) : The Chairman, in the course of an elovent speech, said , Shakespeare had written : "This England never did and l never shall lie at the proud foot of a conquerer but when i she first did help to wound herself." He asked them to consider if England was not wounding herself by her con- -I nection with the drink traffic, and if so, without that wound stannched, she would on some day, perhaps not remote, lie at the proud foot of a conqueror. (Applause.) They heard a good deal of had trade and the moral condition of their society being in danger. The cause in most cases was to , be found in the accursed drink traffic—(hear, Imear)—there- ' fore, as individuals, members of families, and as patriots, they were pledged to the hilt to do away with the system, and he hoped they would give themselves no rest until they succeeded. He was decidedly of opinion that their work could only he accomplished by total ab.tinence. From the most carefully selected s'atistics it was clearly demonstra- ted that moderation had in the past been a failure, and must inevitably be a failure. He was not there to say anything uncharitable of people who took the moderate in, but, as teetotallers they most point out that it was through the channel of moderation that every drunkard bat been taken to his ruin. Teetotalism was not only safe, but decidedly advantageous. The scientific evidence tecently given by the highest authorities conclusively proved that total ab- stinence was on the side of health. Ail udirg to the great poverty existing amongst the masses of the neoele, the Chairman said it was caused largely by the liquor traffic, and of this teetotalers 6hould always make the strongest print. He had only to ask the members of that order dur- ing the next twelve months to push their question to the fore and during the next few years he had hope that their cause would be made One for PerlietiMetary interference. (Aeplanee). . Mr. W. Wightman, Most Worthy Patriarch of Greaf Britain, delivered an address upon the evils resulting from the drink traffic, and his remarks were frequently applauded. Miss Howarth, Grand presiding Sister of the Daughters of Temperance Ualom spoke in favour of that union, as did also Mr. W. H. Lowe, of Manchester. The Rev. W, Veuse said the bad state of trade simply 4neant the enormous traffic in drink. (Applause.) The warehouses of the country wete full of corn, and the cotton and woollen establishments over-crowded with goods. Why was it that food and clothing on the one hand arid countless starving children on the other could not be brought to. gether ? The one thing that kept them apart was the drink traffic, and the only remedy for the bad state of trade was the gospel of temperance. (Atiplause.) On tbe motion of Mr. Withington, seconded by Mr. Heatherington, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to those who had in any way assisted the demonstration, and a similar compliment was paid to those who had addressed the meeting, on the proposition of Mr. Cooke, seconded by Mr. L. M. Temperley. The hearty thanks of those present were also accorded to the Chairman. A choir, conducted by Mr. James Stubbs, rendered several glees daring the evening, and the Mill Brow Brass Band played selections. Mir.s Midwood was at the harmonium. WESTON SONS OF TEMPERANCE. The Nil Desperandten division of the order of Sons of Temperance celebrated their fourth anniversary on Satur- day afternoon by a procession, in which they were joined by the members ot the Cadet section. Fine weather favoured the gathering, and the proceedings were highly successful. The members met at the Wesleyan schools at half-past two, and upwards col 100 formed in processional order. They were headed by the handsome bawler of the Life Boat Crew division, Which had been lent for tl e .purpose, and accom- panied by the Wesleyan Sunday school brass band, con- ducted by Mr. John Ball. The banner cords were held by four young ladies, attired in white (tresses. Admirable order was preserved as the procession passed trough the village, the line being marshalled by Messrs. John Ward and Joseph Lunt, ably assisted by Mr. T. Heesom, of Run- corn. The procession stopped at the houses of the following residents, where the band played various airs I.—Mr J W Kirkham, Mr Thomas Ford, Mr James Detrambin, Mr Wm. Griffiths. Mr James Ford, Mr IV Bankes, J.P., Mr F G Claudet, Mr Robert Price, Mr T Bankes, Mr I Griffiths, Mr E Aaron, Mr W Ormes, and Mrs Kenwright. Tea was pro- vided, under time superintendence of Mr Thomas Ravens- croft, on the return of the procession at the Wesleyan school, the tables being presided over by Mrs Aaron, Mrs Edward Aaron, Miss Annie Smith, Mies Griffiths, Mrs Charles Davies, Mrs Somerville, Miss Hughes, Miss Ford, and Miss Dunbabin. These ladies were assisted by Mrs Price, Mrs Cooper, and Mrs Davidson. Subsequently Mr T Cooke, Grand Scribe of Cheshire, spoke on the benefits derived by membership. He explained that by tke centralisation of the funds the smallest division was placed on an equal financial footing with those which were much larger. On the motion of Mr W Whitehead, seconded by Mr W Norman,a vote of thanks was accorded to the ladies who bad prepared the tea. Mr. Dunbabin replied, after which the members and their friends adjourned to a field, lent by Mr W Bankes, J.P., where the evening was spent in an enjoyable manner. .............—.., ODDPELLOWS' ANNIVERSARY AT Cur..cmaTn.—The members of the City of Refuge Lodge of the Loyal. Order of Oddfellows Friendly Society held their anniversary at the Old Noggin Inn, Culcheth, on Tuesday. The members met at the lodge at nine o'clock, but the morning being wet, a Procession was not formed until about one o'clock, 'which was headed by 14 members on horseback. The route taken by the procession was through Croft and Cul- cheth;and back again to the lodge, calling at several places, ilicluding the residence of Dr. Se.pliton, the medical officer of the lodge. After their return to the lodge, the members sat down to an Qicellent dinner, provided by Mr. Thomas Blackburn, the landlord. The total funds of the society amount to £1,253 b-s 2d. The number of members is about 107. OUTRAGES ON CHILDIIEN : SEVERE CONDFMNATION. —At the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Manisty, Edward Stanley, 63, watch tool maker, of St. Helens, who had been found guilty of attempting to violate a shild, named Eliza Corns, seven years and s-ven months old, at Eccleston, on the 15th July; Thomas Heald, 22, labourer, who had been found guilty of attempting to violate Dorothy Foy, 10 years of ace, at Manchester. on the 20th of July; and Walter Smith, 34. labourer, who had been found guilty of attempting to violate Agnes M.Corkill, a child four years and eight months old, at Manchester, on the 14th of June, were brought forward for sentence. His Lordship said: You three men have been convicted of one of the most abominable crimes that can be committed. It is a most terrible spectacle to see three men committing an offence which brute beasts would scarcely think of commit- ting. Three worse oases could not be imagined. The law does not permit me to pass sentences of penal servitude upon you. , [fit did I should do so. Ido not think the law is severe enough in these cases, and I feel that it must be in- creased, because these crimes on children are becoming a scandal to the country. The sentence upon each of you is that which the law permits me to pass. As 1 have said al reacy I say again—that those outside this court may know it— if these offences go on increasing as they are, the punish- ment will be tremendously increased. The sentence upon each of you is that you be imprisoned for two years with hard labour.

Imerit of metal suasion on the other. But although „men could not now vote they could influence their lem,bands, brothers, sons, and sweethearts. Let the men of ',efteringt„ and of Lancashire put their bands to the plou ee,h and never look back. He would sooner let his right lie.nA wither than vote for the man who would vote for drinleenops to be open' and let little lasses be ruined by vitlians. (Applause.) Let, them see that their representatives in Perliament should be men who would vote for the proteclioe of the young and innocent and go in for the closing of grog shops. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. J. CALVERT propoeed a vote of thanks to Mr. Anderson for Ws address. The Rev.J.YONGIS, in seconding the motion, rejoiced at the unquestioned seccess of the demonstration. Although last year they did well, this year they had done better. (Ap- plause. He understood that they had in the procession 1000 more people than last year, and that in that day's pro- cession walked no less than 3,500 persons. That was some- thing to make the publicans shake in their shoes. He did not wish ill of the publicans as a class of men, but of their trade he did wish ill to the bottom of his heart, believing, as he could not help doing, that there wee no trade in the world so prolific of evil, misery, and distress as the one which they pursued. He thought that if it were not for the ' drink they would not have had to have their feelings har- rowed as they had been during the last three or four weeks by the terrible revelations which had been made of social vice in this coantry. He was sure that if the men and women there assembled had read what the papers had juA ' beeu publishing, they had felt their blood run cold at the revelations that had been placed before them. They formed Bands of Hope to protect the young from the curse of drink, and listened to the cries of boys and girls from the L drunkard's home. But there was another cry of the children . now that entered even more keenly into their hearts than did the other cry. He had looked forward to saying a word, however small it might be, for an expression of feeling on the part of Warrington with regard to these terrible things we had heard about in the last three weeks. He thought it should be arranged that a public meeting should be held in Warrington, a town's meeting presided over by the Mayor, at which men of all classes and sects might meet together to give an utterance of opinion upon the subject. They must pray and work for the time when this dear old land of ours should be spared frem the sin of drink and vice which was day by day eating into its heart and morals. Let every man and woman in Warrington take his and her share in helping on that glorious consummation. He trusted that as years went by that Bend of Hope movement would progress in Warrington, and that drink and drunkenness should in Warrington receive a death blow. (Applause.) Tbe vote of thanks was then cordially pasted. Mr. ANDERSON proposed a vote P: to the Chair- thank e I man. lie referred to the to , ewn 8 meetings held in Liverpool ene to the age of peetection. He hoped that every Sunday sehoolechnrch and chapel, every club, Tory or Radical, would sign Petition; to Parliament en this subject,l and that Warrington would speak Cu'. as well as other towns. "What Lancashire said to day Eogland said to- morrow." Then let them be united. Should they have ' their Band of Hope girls in danger ? They must have the age of protection higher and higher. (Applause.) The Rev. J. McTunn eeconded the resolution. Fifty years ago, he said, weak little temperance societies started for a saber England, and people laughed and said it could not be done. But trial after trial was made, and to-day the , drink traffic of this country perfectly well knew the might of temperance societies. All along the line temperance principles were winning their way, and must succeed. He . then referred to statements given in the Pall Mall pazette ; showing the large increase of abstainers, and a decrease in , the number of licences granted. The increased voting . power of the working classis must further their cause, and , they must as Englishmen resolve that England should yet be sober and pure. (Applause.) The resolution was then carried. Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS, as chairman of the committee, thanked Mr. Naylor fer his presence and great encourage- ment he had given the Union in promising that should the gala prove a financial failure he would be responsible for the deficiency. But it had been a great success. The Union had baen in existence two years, and they had doubled the number of societies connepted with it. (Applause.) The meeting then terminated.

BA TfuLIDAY AT WARRINGTON.

. The baorning of Bank Ruliday opened somewhat inauspieioncly this. 'year, but notwithstanding this there were no signs of any diminution of the popu- larity el the 'holiday. The steady rain which pre- troika during the early part of the day did not pre- vent the people from turning out in large numbers to 'enjoy themselves and to carry out their pre- arranged modes of spending the day. The holiday was very generally observed in the town, all the principal shops, and evidently most of the factories and workshops. being closed. As usual, both the Loudon and North-Western Railway Company and the Cheshire Lines Committee had made suitable pro• visions for carrying exeursionists to various parts of the country. By the London and North- Western line trains were run to London and to 'various towns in the South and Midlands, and places of interest int North Wales; and by the Cheshire Lines there were trains run to Liverpool, Manchester, Southport, and other neighbouring places, and a considerable number were conveyed from the town in this way, though there is little doubt that many were prevented from spendinir the day at distant places by the un- favourable aspect ot the weather in the morning. Frodsham and Lymm were, as usual, well patronised, and the presence of Messrs. Wood's quadrille band, together with the beautiful scenery, drew cr.twds to Belle Monte, Overton Hills. There were also many breaks and other conveyances in use, and by means of these no inconsiderable number of holiday-makers were conveyed to various places around about. In the town the chief attraction was the Band of Hope Union procession and gala, which was very success- ful in every respect, the rainy forenoon having given place to a beautifully fine afternoon before the time fixed for the rendq,voez of the diff-rent detachmeuts of the Union in front a the Town Hall. In addi- tion there were several erMket matches played in the town, which drew together a considerable number of spectators. I,3A.ND OF HOPE DEMONSTIUTION,—PHOCESSION .. .. ..,,... . _
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. There were present Alderman Holmes (who presided in the absence of the Mayor through illness), Aldermen Burgess, Pickmere, Davies, Chandley, Web*ter, and Kean ; Councillors Barker, Greening, Jolley, W. Pierpoint, Roberts, DAM, Marsh, Bolton, Whittle, and Tinsley ; Messrs. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), and Chorlev (borough treasurer).

The minutes of the Museum, Library/ and Arts Cnnmittee and the Cemetery Committee were also confirmed.

come from the baths for the past foa weeks was £33 45 10d, and for the corresponding period last year £4l 15s 6d It was resolved that the baths be closed during the months of June, July, and Auguit at nine o'clock in the evening, except en Wednesday evenings, on which evening and dur- ing the other months of the year they would be closed at eight o'clock. It was also resolved that the borough sur- veyor be empowered to engage the services of an architect to assist him in preparing plans for alterations at the baths.

Alderman PICIChfERE moved, and Councillor BOLTON seconded the confirmation of these minutes. ' Councillor W. PIERPOINT asked as to the meaning of the resolution empowering the surveyor to engage an archi- tect.

Councillor Bovroti explained that the borough sur- veyor's time was so mach occupied with the Longford scheme that he bad not time to attend to the improvements and alteration of the baths. Alderman WEBSTER mentioned that Alderman Pickmere and other gentlemen had visited various public baths in the neighbourhood with a view to the consideration of various improvements, and after discussing the matter it was thought better to get the borough surveyor some temporary assistance. Alderman PICKMERE said the proposed arrangement would not cost very much money, and they would get something like perfection in what they proposed doing. The minutes were then confirmed. MARKETS COMMITTEE. Alderman CHANDLEY, in proposing the adoption of the minutes of this committee, referred to the letter sent:by Mr. Beamont on the subject of the fairs. Mr. Bement some time ago sent a letter on the same subject to the Council, which was duly considered by the committee, but no action was taken in the matter. If it was not out of place it would be of great advantage to the committee to hear any remarks on the subject that might Se made that night. The committee felt some little diffidence in coming to a re- solution in connection with the pleasure fair the last time it was before them, and the same would exist this time. If the Council would express any opinions that they had on the subject of the letter, it would facilitate the deliberations of the Markets Committee. The CHAIRMAN said that although the discussion would be rather out of order it might be allowed under the circuel- I stances. Councillor DAEIN seconded the resolutien. The fair was right enough, but seeing that these accilents had been frequent and of a serious character, he thought the Council would do well to stop the boats. Councillor WHITTLE entirely disagreed with the remarks of Councillor Jolley —(A voice : He is always disagreeing with someone.)—They could not put brains in a man who had none to start with. (Laughter.) If a man wanted to go into a swing boat, he must do it. They night just as well try and force a man not to go in a railway train or a steam boat, as he was just as liable to accident. Ile con- sidered it very silly to attempt to do anything in this matter. Alderman WEBSTER said that in cases where accidents oc- curred through persons being intoxicated, they must take the consequences. The only remedy he could think of was more stringent bye-laws. The Warrington Bald of Hope lJaidil On Monday held their second demonetratiott anti g' ala which, favoured dur- ing the afternood and evening by fins Weather, proved a great cuccess. The Various Bands of Hope incorporated in the Unien Met early in the afternoon on the green in front Of the Town Hale where a procession was formed. The '<Molars, teachers, and others who toek part in the procession numbered no less than 3,500 persons, and the banners and bannerettes carried were numerous. The order of procession of the various contingents was as follewe : (1) l'xials'-green, with Workhouse band; (2) Latchford, with Temperance Mission Band; (3) Bald-street ; (4) Bank Quay ; (5) Golborne-street; (6) Emmanuel; (7) Legh.stteet, with band; (8) Howley, nsith band ; (9) Cock- hedge ; (10) Silver-street ; (11) P.nekley-street, with band ; (12) St. Paul's, with band • (13) Wycliffe, with band. The procession left the park by the entrance nearest Market Gate and proceeded by way of Sankey-street, Legh-street, Edgeworth-street, liewsey-street, Tanners-lane, Winevick- street, liorsemarket-street, and Bridge-street to a field at Wilderspool-causeway. The route taken was thronged with observers, and the various streets mentioned were busy, not only during the progress of the procession, but for some- time previous and afterwards. Complete arrangements had been tnade for ensusing the success of the gala, and the pro- gramme drawn up was an ambitious one, including, in ad- dition to a number of races for boys and girls, a brass band 'contest for which four entries were received, and singing and reciting contests. The events, some of which were contested in several heats, numbered twelve, and were so miscellaneous in character as to provide a very fruitful source of entertainment. In addition enterprising csterers had at one end of the field established the ad- juncts of a miniature fair, and were repaid by a thriving business. At several well-stocked stalls substantial edibles were vended, and the 'inner man was by no means neglec- ted. It is estimated that over 10,1t00 people were admitted lathe field, the approach to which was crowded, and at that part of the deer when the nzmber present was highest •end busiest, the gala field prevented a sight to be viewed nith pleasure.
