NOTES BY 'THE WAY.

Judging from the fact that the T:otts committee have held a meeting to consider the advisability of arranging fixtures with -Lancashire for next season, it is quite evident that their supporters are tiredmf the position taken up by the authorities. The meeting tcok place on Satrrday, but the decision arrived at is not one that will be well received in the County 'Palatine, or conducive to the settlement of the questien. It was argued that now Crossland had been got rid of the obotacle had 4.. wen removed,...nd the presump- tion was that Lancashire woald be glad to accept the fix- ture. We are. however, inclined to think that in Ws they will be mistaken. It was decided " that the committee be ,empowered ta coafer with theavammittee of the Kent Cricket -Club with regard to playing matches with Lancashire, an i he empowered to act as they think best in the interects of county cricket and cricket in general." This loan very well, but the Notts committee will find. that they .cannot Lave quite all their own way. On Bank Holiday Derbyshire attd Lancashire began their return at Derby. The home county being fire to bat scored 108. When Monday's play ceased Lancashire had lord seven wickets for 149 ; end rain interfered so much On Tuesday that a start was impracticable until half-past three in the afternoon, the Lancashire innings being brought to a close for 180 runs. On Wednesday the gam was concluded, Lancashk-e winning by ten wickets. The Canterbury Week was opened by the return between Kent and Yorkshire. Kent went in to bat and kept pos- session all the afternoon, having lost seven wickets for 209 mos when the stumps were drawn for the day. Rain caused the play to be delayed bare until half-past two o'clock, and a little over an hour's play saw the finish of the Kent in- nings for 312 runs. The visitors started about four o'clock, and seven wickets were down for 116 runs when Tuesday's play ceased. A storm passed over Canterbury on Wednesday, preventing play until three o'clock, when Yorkshire completed the first innings for 138, and had to follow on, the match ending in a draw. Hampshire and Sussex commenced their return at South- ampton, before a large company. The home team bitted first, but did not score largely. Hants scored 153. Ibis was topped by 13 runs by Sussex. In the second innings of Hants 258 were scored, and as Sussex could only place 144 against this, they were defeated by 101 runs.

.. At a meetin.; of the schools Committee, held on the 4th Auzust, present the Rev. G.F. Roberta (chairman), Messrs. Derbyshire, W. Boughton, J. Houghton, Broadbent, and Foster. The committee had befere them the plans ap- proved by the Local Government Board, and the clerk hav- ing read the correspondence and suggestions by the architeo• turd department to extend, if practicable; the distance of pigstyes and stables from the present buildings. and Mr. Owen advising it to be practicable, the committee author- ised him to extend the distmca by 5 feet, making a total distance of 3:5 feet. Other suggestions by the same depart- ment being also practicable, it was decided to act upon them, Mr. 0 weu also produced the specifications prepared by him, and the same was approved after being read and carefully considered. Mr. Owen was authorised to prepare an adver- tisement to builders and contractors for tenders for the bai.dings, the tenders to be laid before the Guardians at their next Board meeting. It was recommended that the £1,400 to be borrowed to repay the Public Works Loan Board, and the £l,OOO to carry out the new works at the schools be obtained, and that the .£l,OOO be repaid in the manner provided by law as to the £1,400 and in the same periol—The CHAIRMAN moved the confir- mation of these minutes.—Mr. RATCLIFFE called attention to the dry rot at the schools, which he considered to be vary serious.—The CHAIRMAN said the committee had not been able to deal with that matter at their last meeting, but they hoped to do so at their next.—Mr. JOLLEY thought it would perhaps satisfy Mr. Ratcliffe if he told him it Wag A Yen' email thing, and ha I been attended I, Dy e lecal joiner,— Mt.)3R°49/174U "laded. #.1...7, inalrman's proposal, which was agriAtc.

Pit/OATH SCHOOLS —S2OOIOL'S CHARGES. Tilt CLERK read a communication which by the direcion of the Board he had sent to the Local Government Board de- tailing the action taken by the Board in consequence of the Complaints of the Local Government Board inspector, Mr. Henley, as to the Padgate schools, and mentioning that the , Guar/tans had resolved that it was advisable to have sepa- rate medical officers for the Padgate schools and the work- house. The Clerk read a copy of a letter which lead been forwarded by Dr. Spinks to the Local Government Board in reply to the above.mentioned letter. He stated that on the day of Mr. Henley's visit to the schools there we're only five cages of scabies or itch on the books. Unfortunately he (Dr. Spines) was not present to point out to Mr. Henley the difference between itch and other postules, consequently he mistook six cases of postules for itch. The itch Cases were all cured in a week, so that in the month of May there were only two fresh caees. and none in June or up, to the present data. Mr. Henley's principal complaint was that he (Dr. Spinks) (lid not send ;he cases to the hospital and so isolate them. His reason for not doing to was en account of the hospitals being too far from the homes, and there was not proper care or supervision of the child:en, or means of classifying them ; and, further, theta was only one yard and one closet for both males and females. Last November he found two of the oldest girls in the cloeet With four boys, two of whom were inside and two at the doer preventing the girls from coming out. They were making a great noise, and on asking the girls what all the noise was about and why they were there, the reply was the boys in. side were behaving indecently. That was his principal reason for not using the hospital. Another reason was the great danger from fire, as he had found a little girl burnt across the abdomen, she having fallen against the bars of the grate. Again, the children ran about the fields in their night clothes, there being no proper person to look after them during the day time as the woman (who was almost a cripple) woreed in the laundry all day, a girl of twelve being left in charge during her absence, the committee being uniiilling to em- ploy a proper person to attend to the place. He therefore considered it better to leave the hospital empty rather than run the risk of a coroner's inquest. Mr. Spinks enclosed a statement showing that itch was more prevalent in the spring and autumn months, and also stated that it was not at any time introduced by fresh arrivals of children from the Workhouse. It was confined to two or three families who must have caught the infection when visiting their friends. Respecting Mr. Henley's statement that the medical officer of the Workhouse should not be medical officer of the schools, Mr. Spinks said ha had always t titer] the greatest care of the children both at the Workhouse and at the schools, and that for the last six years there had been no epidemic amongst them, and not a single case of the death of a child of school age. The Clerk to the Guardians in giving the report of the proceediags of the Board meet- ing on the 27th of May had said that the minutes of the School Committee were adopted after a vote on an amend- ment which was lost by 14 to 4. That majority was no , doubt influenced by the Chairman relating the eaft of a boy who was brought from the Workhouse and was the day after sent to the school hospital. This statement, he (Dr. Spinks) maintained was not according to fact, and he had no doubt the voting would have been different had the correct state of the facts been known as several of the Guar- dians expressed themselves so, some of them stating that the clerk should not have sent the papers to the Local Govern. ment Board until the instructions given by the School Committee on June 9th were confirmed by the Boa, el cf Guardians at their meeting on the 10th, and were disap- pointed that he had not done so. In conclusion, Mr. Spines I said he had In no way neglected the children or failed it his duty towards them, but bad treated them in the best I wooer eCe9rding PePP e"ln?.il A hio diePeeal, The I hospital wae net t fit place for children of both Sexes, par- ticularly when there was no. proper supervision, fle also attached some extracts taken from his reports to the com- mittee at various times complaining priuelpally of the state of the yards, and said nothing had been done to remedy it. —The (Akita next read Mr. Minesb (superintendent of the Padgate Schools) reply to Dr. Spinks, in which he stated that the remarks Made by that gentleman in his letter to the Local Government Board were ealculated to endangef. the reputation of the schools and alas reflected on their management. In justice, therefore, to the Committee of management, to the officers of the 'achools, and to the ehi:dren committed to their charges it was his duty to sub. mit the following observations ; Firstly, as regarded the I alleged indecency on the pa ti bi some of the children as a reason why he discarded the use of the hospital he wished to point out that during the month of November last there was only one little girl named Rhoda Roughley, aged siN years, on the doctor's hook, and she was not permanently confineil to. the lectanital. Daring that part of November only two lath boys were in the hospital and alrother was tilmitted on the 11th, and another on the 18th el November. One of them was discharged on that date, rid the others on the 27th November, and on the foliose:lt day three girls were admitted to the hospital. It was tlesr, therefore, from those data there could riot have beereenore than one little girl aged six years and two little btree, both in petticoats, who were all classed as infants, in fhe hospital at any one time during the month of November. Ile had questioned the foster parents and other officers re- garffing the statement made by Mr. Spinks, and they were unanimous in declaring they had never witnessed or heard of the slightest act of indecency among the children under their charge. The doctor had never before made such a charge or assigned any such reason for not visiting the hospital, and when visiting he had invariably been accom- panied by the matron or Mrs Lindsay, or himself (Mr. Mines). Referring to the case of a child who was once burnt in one of the hospital wards, it was true that a little girl, when playing with two other girls received a bumn whilst the woman in charge was absent in the hospital lava- atory ; but this was on the 14th of October, 1883, and at a time previous to tire guards being provided for the holiital. These were supplied more than twelve mouths prior to Mr. Henley's visit to the schools, and a woman had been con- stantly in attendance at the hospital during the whole of that peritd, so that when there had been cases in the hospi- tal the reason given by Mr. Spinks ceuld not be the one pre- venting the use of the hospital. In truth it was almost constantly in use during the whole of that time. Mr. Spinks also complained of some children who ran about the field in tneir night-clothes. She watched girls leaving factories on wags days, and entering into conversation wirh them, contrived to pos- sess herself of their wages. The magistrates on Tuesday ' sent her to a reformatory for four years. LORD SALISBURY ON FOREIGN BOUNTIES. - The Mal- gals of Salisbury on Wednesday received at the Foreign Office a large deputation of workingmen delegates,,who de- sired to point out the injury inflicted on British la,.sour by the foreign bounty system in connection with the sugar trade, and suggested as a remedy a countervailing duty on bounty-aided sugars. Lord Salisbury said he did not need the presence of such a deputation to convince him that great suffering exists in this industry. His opinion was that the power of modifying our fiscal system in order to defeat any oppressive action on the part of foreign countries was a power which ought to be rarely exercised, but which ought to be possessed, and if it was known that it was pos. sessed it would be very seldom nec,eisary to exercise it. He was far from advocating a general practice of retaliatory tariffs, and still farther from advocating anything approach.. ing to protection ; but be believed that freedom from self- imposed trammels of particular theories TM necessary if we meant to (hal with the world as it la, and it was only by a free and bold action in this respect that they could obtain that equality which was their natural and legitie mate desire. He hoped foreign Powers might be induced to abandon this system of bounties, which was not good for themselves and which • was deeply injurious to us.

Mn. CHAMBERLAIN AT Hutt.—Mr. Chamberlain spoke at a great meeting of Liberals held on Wednesday evening in Hengler's Circus, Hull, in support of the local candi- date. Replying to a vote of confidence in the Liberal leaders, the right hon. gentleman said he would not con- ceal his opinion that the pace of reform in the future would be quicker than it had been in the past. Everywhere there was discussion and hope and expectation, and it would be dangerous to disappoint that hope. The Liberal party had by recent changes secured a vantage ground which he him- self had hardly ever dared to anticipate. His wildest ex- pectations had been exceeded, and he was hopeful that at last the social evils which disgraced our civilisation and the wrongs which had cried vainly for redress would find a hearing and a remedy. This was a turning point in our political history, and if people were couteut with old formulas and watchwords, the Reform agitation would have been a barren and unprofitable business. He desired them to consider the privations and misery associated with the excessive inequality in the distribution of riches, and if the Legislature could do something to elevate the condition of the people, to give them means of enjoyment and opportu- nities of improvement, they would do more for the pros- perity and morality of the country than could be achieved by any laws for the prevention of excess and crime. The right hon. gentleman, in the course of his further remarks, spoke in favour of free education, and maintained the cor- rectness of his contention that the rich were taxed too little and the poor too much. He also strongly urged the necessity of a reform of the land laws. On athursday evening Mr. Chamberlain, speaking at Hull, referred to the necessity for union in the Liberal party. He said there were persons calling themselves Whigs who would, if they could, thrust the Radicals from the party. The Radicals were prepared to limit their action to what was the average opinion of the whole party at any given time, but they, as the pioneers of the party, would not give up their right of free discussion. He commented on the practical unanimity of feeling be- tween himself and the Tory Democrats, and thought the moderate Liberals, if they left the Radicals, would not fare any better in company with the Tories. It was gratifying to find that the late Government's foreign policy was being scrupulously followed by Lord Salisbury, and one satisfac- tory result of the change of administration had been the restoration of the order and dignity of the lieuse of Com- mons.

As a matter of fact, legislation has this year out- 1 I run supply. In ordinary sessions a Government is careful to get all its Bills in so forward a state that the moment the last vote is taken in supply the business of the session is practically over. It fre- quently happens that the proceedings in respect of the Appropriation Bill are so purely formal that the House adjourns two or three days in sifccession, having sat only the few minutes necessary to ad- vance the Appropriation Bill by a stage. But to- day the House has its hands full of work, gets at it early, sticks to it late, and begins again the next day. The fact is, opposition in the ordinary sense of the word is effaced in the House of Commons. A Conservative Government is content to do the work of a Liberal Opposition, and the Opposition is, naturally enough; quiet and satisfied. All the measures that have occupied the attention of the House during the past ten days are of Liberal birth. In some cases, as in respect of the Telegraphs Bill, the Government have for appearances, sake intro- I driced some variation; but when the Opposition put I up their back they have dropped the amendment and gone back to the old lines of the Bill. The opportunity is a rare one for dealing with abuses, and it has been fully utilised. The object of the Government, of course, is to have a good show of work to display before the electors when they go to the country, and so that the work is good no one will grudge them the opportunity. The nomination of Captain Gosset as K.C.B. has given universal satisfaction in the House of Com- mons. It will be difficult at first to change the long familiar appellation of Captain Gosset for Sir Robert. But this inconvenience will be lessened by the fact that the old Sergeat-at-Arms passeth away ;with the old order of things, and everything will be new, the Parliament, the times, and the Sergeant-at- Arms. With the old Sergeant-at-Arms there will disappear a Parliamentary institution of which out- siders know nothing but the name. This is Gosset's room, where many a keg of whisky has been drunk, many a box of cigars smoked, and many a story told. The..new Sergeant takes over the apartments of the old one, and with them the ante-chamber en- deared by many memories of cheerful nights gone by. Mr. Erskine is a man of very different tempera- ment from Captain Gosset. His courtesy is un- deniable, but he is of a less genial nature than the jolly old Sergeant whom Punch this week, in a pathetic picture, shows locking up for the last time the door of Parliament. I don't know whether he ' smokes, and am sure, that though a Scotchman, he does not drink whiskey; whilst he has no taste for the full flavoured conversation of " Gosset's room." Possibly Mr. Frank Gosset, Sir Robert's son, the newly-appointed Deputy Sergeant, may find some room where the family tradition may be kept up. But these kind of things ill bear translation. The excitement which kept both Houses of Par- liament and all London Society on the qui vive in connection with a great scandal has sensibly de- creased. Last week every night had its report that action had been taken in the courts of law, and the publication of alleged facts which had, in truth, long ceased to be private, was looked for every morning in the papers. The subject is a difficult one to treat. It is impossible to ignore it; for a fortnight it has been the one subject of conversa- tion' and there is scarcely a paper in the country that has not had a more or less veiled reference to it. I feel the less hesitation in alluding to it here, because in doing so I am able to state that there is not a word of truth in the monstrous story from beginning to end. It originated from a bubble born in the brain of a hysterical woman, excited by t he flood of prurient print with which the country has lately been whelmed. When the story first came out it was dressed up with the most fantastic exaggeration. The original charge was not enough to suit the ap- petite of the hour, and all kinds of monstrous par- ticulars were added. The scandal received its first check from disclosure of the fact that the date fixed for what was alleged to have taken place went back more than a year. The gossips had assumed that it was a matter of recent date, had in fact happened within the past few days,and had ramifications in the direction of the revelations of an evening paper. Finding themselves wrong on one important point, the thought obtruded itself that possibly they were wrong on others. This suspicion has grown till there is to-clay quite a revulsion of feeling, and peo- ple are saying that perhaps after all there is nothing in it, which in truth there is not. I gave the other week a list of names which the fashionable world affect to pronounce in a manner to which the spelling gives no clue. At dinner the other night I note 4 a coincidence which forcibly brought this eccentricity to mind. I had the plea- sure of sitting next to Mr. Boughton, who, if he had not been a successful painter, would have made his repiWation as a writer; whilst immediately oppo- site was Lord Houghton. It will be observed that except for the initial letter these names are spelt exactly- alike- Then *why should• the painter call himself Barton and the poet stjle himself Howton? It is one of the things that no fellow can under- stand, though it is a puzzle older than our genera- tion. In Thackeray's time there was a litterateur named Angus Reach. Ile wrote chiefly novels such as "Clement Lorimer," now, like himself, dead and forgotten. It was Mr. Reach's peculiarity to pro- nounce his name as if the final letter were "k." Thackeray, sitting at a certain dinner, persistently called him Mr. Reach. At last the novelist could stand this no longer, and he petulantly said "Reack, if you please, Reack." Thitckeray said nothing at the moment. But after a while observing a dish of peaches near the novelist, he called out in a tone designed to be heard all over the table "Mr. Reack will you, if you please, pass me a peack." I learn from a private letter from San Francisco that Monsignor Capel is now in that city, where he has been residing for some months. A more recent arrival is the Marquis of Queensbury, and the oddest thing of all is that the Marquis and the Monsignor have been engaged ia public disputation on the question of agnosticism. The Marquis was no match for the Monsignor, who speedily disposed of his ar- guments. What a strange combination of circum- stances that should bring these men, each remarka- ble in his way, talking about agnosticism by the Golden Gate. The Marquis of Queensburywas a more familiar figure in sporting circles than in that to which his rank might have entitled him. But for ,_aaale years there was no more familiar figure in the "est/London, drawing-rooms than that of the hand- -B°,.tme; welb:bred, -habile Monsignor, whose sudden ulaapPearance,. to turn up again in America. has puzzled many people. - Marlb°rough House is to be enlarged. The Prince of Wales would not ask for a grant for his son on attaining his majority, and Prince Albert Victor can not actually have a separate estate. But his father will do the most he can for him. The young prince will remain under the paternal roof, but the roof ; will have to be enlarged and resisted. Marlborough Howe is really but a small palace, and its capabili- ties have been seriously strained even to attain its present accommodating retinae for the youn power. With an additional g prince addition becomes a necessity—in the case of the building also. Parlia- ment has granted £5,000, so that the contractor's men may set to work when London empties.
Lincoln's Inn, August 4.

ST. HELENS POLITICAL NOTICES. Sir,—ln front of the St. Helens Town Hall is a notice board on which "public notices," or at least notices affect- ing corporate matters requiring publicity, are usually posted. Hitherto, so far as my experience teaches, it has been reserved for such announcements, but during the pre- Sent week I have been surprised to see a big flaming placard i in blue letters, calling upon the Tories of the district to see 'to the proper registration of their votes. Surely, sir, I think this is prostituting Corporation and public property to poli- tical ends and aims, and if the " borough " notice board is to be used for political purposes, I should suggest that one Ibe provided for each party—namely, Tory, Radical, the Fourth party, and even the Irish Land Leaguers. Then the Corporation might go a little further, and provide a simi- lar board for each religions sect and denomination, and if they were made of a fancy design they would tend ti still further improve and beautify our handsome Town Hall. The Town Council appear to be taking great interest in decorating the " interior " of the edifice, but, air, I think it remarkably strange that not one of our representatives appears to have thought of the idea of decorating the front of the building In the manner I have suggested. However, sir, I should not personally wait for the cerporation to move in the mat- ter, but I strongly urge upon the Liberal Association er the National Reform Union to instruct one of their men to proceed with a can of paste, a big brush, and cover all the board, front and back, the latter for the instruction of the clerk!, who would be able to read it from the Town Hall windows, with monstre red placards, urging upon the " rate- payers " to support the candidature of Colonel Gamble. I am prompted to ask why have not the Irish seized thif op- portunity of thus proclaiming the virtues of their leader, Mr. Parnell? That is a surprise to me. But, perhaps, it was a corporate oversight; nevertheless I would strongly urge the Liberal council to see the necessity of at once mov- ing In so important a matter. What, is Councillor R. P— going to allow the Tories to monopolise the " public " boards in that manner? One would have thought that he above all others would have prevented it, or ,at least have seen that the objectionable placard was removed.—Yours, truly, St. Helens, 6th August, 1885. A RADICAL.

Sir,—! see in your paper Ta-ir-e-a—t pother being made about the stoppage or attempted stoppage of a footpath OR CO Morley Common. Fortunately for his peace of mind, dear Sir Gllbert never reads the Examiner. Oh no! he never reads it; its type is never seen within the bounds of Walton where all t,Jings are 80 green. The proverbial philosopher s sid that "Where ignorance is bliss 'tis folly to be wise." Being always glad to see, appreciate, and acknowledge the smallest evidences of wisdom even iu a political opponent, I commend our Tory candidate's wisdom ix thus avoiding having certain disagreeable facts and assertions thrust upon his notice. He can thus leave to an agent the disagreeable duty of denying facts and statements which he as a man of honour could not conscientiously deny. This is a very convenient arrangement. You give the hint to your agent, whose abilities (including conscience) you buy at -- per annum. He then denies the facts which he knows to be true, and makes assertions which he knows to be false. Now this in politics is not called lying; it is merely a dexterous concealment of the truth and a clothing of falsehood in the Rub of veracity. Of course Sir Gilbert (what a delight it Is t'. me to write this title, recalling as it does the eminent ' public services for which it was conferred) knows nothing of this. Indeed I have heard him say himself—"l am not supposed to know anything of this." It was about election time and was said to a possibly too importunate supporter, whose greed was greater than his modesty aad discre- i tion. _ _ - .

In regard to this footpath-stopping, I would ask Sir Gil- bert Greene!' throu4h any of hut friends who may see this, if he can say with truth that he never stopped a footpath from Appleton through the Denna to Hatton? This public right and convenience I was in the habit of using some twenty summers ago with profit and delight, and was told by the old inhabitants that it had been a public road fer fifty years. It is now closed for the repose and reproduc- tion of the sacred p'ieasant. Is this so or is it not ? Will Sir Gilbert Greenall answer? No agents need reply. In this I deal with principals only. if Sir Gilbert himself says he never ordered, sanctioned, or permitted this viola- tion of a public right I shall be bound to give to that asser- tion the credence due to the word of a gentleman. Other- wise silence assents.—l am, sir, yours &c., JOHN PEERS. Greenbank, Penketh, August Bth, 1885.

Sir,—lf any confirmation were wanting of my statement that the recent issuing of a scurrilous handbill was the out- come of Radical malicitnisness it is to be found in the prompt manner in which the Liberal agent, Mr. Roberts, has come forward to defend " A voice fr...m the crowd and to deny the truth of what I have asserted in this matter. Mayhap there is a still closer connection between Mr. Roberta and the author of the kandhill than I have even yet hinted at. Mr. Roberts, with that ingenuity and perversion of fact which Is so characteristic of the Radical party, attempts to controvert my statements seriatim. It is useless to argue with him in a matter of this kind, but I wish to state that I re-affirm as absolutely correct everything I have already stated, and am able to produce witnesses to prove that I am right in every particular. Furthermore, I have Sir Gilbert Crreenall's permission and authority to say that so far as he is personally concerned, he not only never gave any orders or made any request that the footpath should be closed, but that when the matter was brought up he was utterly at a hiss to know what footpath was alluded to, as it had entirely escaped his memory that there was a footpath of any kind in the place referred to, not having fired a shot in the vicinity for very many years. As regards my "delusions," which Mr. Roberts is pleased to mention, I may say :-1. hat,as the last election took place previous to my coming to Warrington, I am in no way re- sponsible for the minority in which the Conservatives from various causes, then found themselves. 2. lhat at the re- visions of 1882, 1883, and 1894 there was a considerable, and in the latter year a large, Conservative gain. 3. That at the South-West Ward contest, between Messrs. Wright aad Bowden, the Conservative candidate was elected in spite of the Liberal forecast that he would be defeated by 30. 4. That at the last election of Guardians, although it was confidently asserted that none but Liberals would be elected, four Conservatives ;were put in for Warrington and four for out-townships, which had previously returned Liberals. 5. That at all the recent contests in the South- East Ward the Conservative candidates have been elected. 6. That at the election of assistant overseer the Liberals chose to introduce a political feeling and to bring out a can- didate in opposition to the man who had held the post and done the work well for years, whereupon the Conservatives espoused his cause.' and gave the Radicles another good thrashing. 7. That at the last contested election in the South-West Ward the Liberals were snaking bets of 5 to 1 against us, but we returned our candidate with a still larger majority than before. So much for some of my "delusions." I may have others, but I am not under the "delusion " that large numbers of respectable working-men are wilfully deceiving me when they tell me repeatedly that, though they voted Radical at the last election, they shall not do so again ; nor am I under the delusion " that respectable working-men will be deluded into withdrawing their support from Sir Gilbert Greenall in consequence of the mean, cowardly, and urtrne attack that has been made upon him recently. I think I know something of the mind of Warrington working- men, and I venture to predict that the result of Mr. Roberts' move in this matter will he just the contrary of what he expect., and he will be forced to admit, after the general election taking place in November, that I was not under a " delusion" when I affirmed, as I do now, that it is the de- termination of the working-men of Warrington, by a large majority, to once again, in spite of the venomous and anonymous attacks of the Radical!, to return to Parlia rant their old and tried friend Sir Gilbert Greenall, who is one of the greateet benefactors Warrington has ever had.— Yours truly, JOHN HAMPSON, Conservative Agent. Conservativo Club, 7th August. 1885.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGITST 8, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGITST 8, 1885.
TRIAL AND SENTENCE OF RICHARD
SPANN.

At the Liverpool Summer Assizes on Tuesday. in the I Crown Court, St. George's Hall, before Mr Justice Manisty, Richard Spann, 36 years of age, wheelwright, was indicted on a charge of having, at Warrington, on the 4th March, 1885, and on other days within four months before the presentation of a bankruptcy petition, unlawfully and fraudulently removed divers of his goods, to the value of .£lO and upwards, contrary to sub-section 5, section 11, of the Debtors' Act, 1869; and also of baying committed vari- ous offences contrary to the same Act. The indictment I contained numerous counts. Mr. Smylv and Mr. Pickford (instructed by Mr. Percy Davies) conducted the prosecu- tion, and Mr. Cottenham (instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne) defendod.—Mr. Smyly, in opening the case, said the indict- ment charged the prisoner, Richard Spann. with having committed various offences under sections and sub-secti ,us of the Debtors' Act. He then proceeded to give details of the case, which have been previously reported in our columns. _ _ _

The first witness called was Edward Josep's Nicholson, who was examined by Mr Pickford. He said he WAS a solici- tor and registrar to the Warrington County. Court. Toe witness deposed as to the filing of the petition and statement of affairs presented by the bankrupt. Thomas Joseph Ridgway, official receiver, of Warrington, stated that on the sth March last the prisoner filed a peti- tion. On the 9th March a statement of affairs, bearing that date, was produced to him, and sworn to by him. On the • 6th March, the day after the receiving order, he asked the prisoner if he had any other goods besides those which he bad given LID to his assistant. The prisoner replied that he had not. For the stock he received £lB7 14a liii, and for the furniture £23 17s 10d. After he took possession there woes second statement of affairs made. The prisoner then esti- mated his stock to produce £45. The second valuation was made in order to enable witness to make a reoort to the creditors. John Edward Wright, a surveyor, put in a plan of the prisoner's premises. James Chapman said he was a wheelwright, and that prior to the sth March he was in the prisoner's employ. He had been in his employ for about four years, and he was foreman of the wheelwright's shop. He left on the sth. March last. He remembered on that date the prisoner coming into tlak shop saying he bad filed a petition and must stop work at once. Before that be received instruc- tions from the prisoner with reference to certain property. Witness, with a man named Joseph Bridge, a blacksmith in the employ of the prisoner, removed a quantity of the pri- soner's geode, by the prisoner's directions. Witness took goods to the value of £lB to Cross's on the 3rd March, and on the 4th March witness and Bridge took some goods to Ashton's. Witness also took some tools to a neighbour named Clarke. The tools would be about £4 in value. Witness next gave particulars of certain property whieh was concealed underneath the floors of the prisoner's premi- ses, and to a quantity of paint being concealed underneath the p tint room. -, Joseph Bridge, a blacksmith, formerly in the employ of the prisoner, said he removed certain goods along with Chapman by the prisoner's direction. William Mallard, deputy official receiver of Warrington, said that between the sth March and the 30th April, the property which had been removed by previous wit- nesses was not disclosed to him. But subsequently the prisoner acknowledged to having concealed a portion of the goods. Joseph Hewitt said he went into possession of the pri- soner'e premises on the 10th June by order of the Official Receiver. He found concealed in a loft, underneath some straw, 14 pair of gig shafts and bends. In another place he found 19 pair of cart shafts, which were covered over with straw. Nadi tniel Clarke, formerly an apprentice of the prisoner, gave evidence to show that the prisoner had concealed some goods on his premises. Mr. Cottenham said he intended to raise a paint of law. He submitted that the annulment of the original bankruptcy extinguished the present offence, and that therefore the present prosecution could not be maintained. Thl jury found the prisoner guilty on the facts, and his Lordship said the legal argument could be brought before him next day. The case came on at the Assizes on Wednesday morning, but was again adjourned. On Thursday, Mr. Cottenham, who defended, argued at some length the point of law he raised in the prisoner's favour. His Lordship ruled against Mr. Cottenham, saying that it WAS a very clear case, and that he really could have no doubt about it. Mr. Cottenisam urged on behalf of the prisoner that he had already been in prison for five weeks. His Lordship, in addressing the prisoner, said: The jury have found you guilty of several offences against the Act of Parliament to which 1 have just referred, viz., the Debtors' Act of 1869, which has very stringent clauses for the pur- pose of preventing these offences. That Act was passed to protect those unfortunate persons who ale creditors of • bankrupt, and in order to ensure that everything has been given up to the creditors honestly and in a straightforward rummer, and above all without resorting to the means of which you have been guilty. It is about as audacious a fraud as has corns under my notice for a very long time, and I am also very sorry to think that you should endeavour to implicate others who were your servants, and who were to' a peculiar position, assisting you under yout. orders to do wrong. Certainly, it does not improve your position that such an attack was made upon the servants who did assist you to commit this wrong. I shall not, however, allow this consideration to influence me In the sen- tence. But avert from that, you secreted property to a very considerable extent, and I cannot forget, also, that the so doing involves falsehood and perjury, be- cause you rendered an account and swore you had given up everything yen bad in your possession. It is a very serious crime, and I look in vain for any circumstances to mitigate it. The law says that in the case of a bankrupt doing what you did, a very heavy punishment indeed may be inflicted. I am not going to enforce the full penalty of the law, but I cannot pass this over with a light sentence. This is not only an attempt to defraud, but is is fact larceny, perjury, falsehood, and fraud. I shall take into account the fact of your already being imprisoned for floe weeks. The usual sentence in a case of this kind is a term of imprisonment for eighteen months to two years, with hard labour; but under all the circumstances I may reduce it to the very lowest limit. You most ;be imprisoned and kept to hard labour for ten calendar months. The prisoner was then removed.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD MEETING.
div.p: LOCAL BOARD MEETING.

The monthly-rn-e-etirTg-w-ae6e-id-iWt-he-Ofine at Lymm, on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Cameron, there being also present—Messrs. Thomason, Rogers. Hall, Appleton. Woolley, Forster, Gibbon, Ridgway (clerk), and Dr. Fox (medical officer Of health). At a previous meeting of the Board Mr. Rogers made some remarks in reference to the Medical Officer of Health, who was not then present, and Dr. Fox now referred to the obloquy that he had had to submit to in consequence of those remarks, which had Leen freely disseminated throughout Cheshire. Distinct notice was given that at the next meeting it should be moved that his appointment and connection with t,he district should ,terminate—the district of Lymm, in which he had lived for over seven years, taking from the township the large amount of £lO a year, and spending in it perhaps £6OO a year. It , was not always easy to leave a place where one had formed , a connection, and the notice of motion given could not have been more severe had he been a feloo, or disgraced himself in the most abject manner. He thought he should be allowed to save himself from comments that had been made in the matter. He had insisted, from a feeling of duty, upon some arrangement regarding the important mat- ter of scavenging. Dr. Fox having spoken on that subject, explained that it was impossible for him to be present at , the last meeting. Mr. Rogers took advantage of the ter- minable nature of his (Dr. Fox's) appointment to give notice of motion that it should terminate, because of a more , difference of judgment ukon an important matter, a differ- ence in which be thought he should have as fair and reason- , able a chance as Mr. Rogers. These appointments were not made terminable at the end of five years to give opportunity to a tyrannical person, who would domineer over every per- son on the Board, of getting an officer out of his place. It was because there was legislation in the near future with regard to the arrangement of sanitary districts, and if ap- pointments such as his were made life appeint- mente there would in a new arrangement of districts always be the difficulty of vested interests and compensation of permanent officials. He could not imagine a greater want of good taste than to make use of that, as it were accidental power placed in the hand of any member who liked to exercise it, to injure a man who was acting with highly conscientious motives. He wished to say that he had received such systematic obstruction from Mr. Rogers that he had twice brought his resignation in his pocket. After what bad occurred he was in a manner put upon his trial, and could no longer send in his resignation. —A rather heated discussion followed, and Mr. Hall re- marked that there was a certain amount of hole and corner work went on„ at the Board that should be put a stop to. They should work pleasantly together, but so long as he was on the Board he would allow no one to domineer over him.—The subject was soon afterwards allowed to drop.-- The Medical Officer then read his report, whic's stated that during the half-year which terminated the 30th June, 1885, there were registered 47 deaths, at all ages, and from all causes, in the district of the Lecal Board. This was / qui• valent to an annual death-rate of 200 Der 1,000. Of the 47 deaths 15 were of aged persons, and 16 of infants under the first year of age. Number of births registered during halt- year was 76, the annual birth-rate of 32.3. P,r- centage of births over deaths, 29 ; percentage of infantile deaths to total births 21.0 exactly.— The Chairman read a letter from the Rev. G. W. Guest, rector, complaining of the obstruction caused by the rush- bearing erections, swieg boats, ikc. Rush-bearing, with its attributes, was becoming el serious nuisance to the peace of the village, and it was time steps were taken for its removal, especially from the village, where the space was entirely in- , adequate.—After a long conversation Mr. Rogers proposed, ,

and Mr. Woolley seconded, "that notice be served upon all I persons who obstruct the highway with their shows, &c., to remove such obstructions, and, failing removal thereof, that the clerk is Instructed to summons all such persons for ob- structioes at the next sessions."—The resolution was car- ried, the chairman and Messrs. Rogers, Woolley, Forster, and Gibbon voting in favour of it, and none voting against it. Messrs. Hall, Appleton, and Thomason declined to vote. —Mr. Hall brought forward the subiect of an alleged taking in of land by Messrs. Gibbon, and, an explanation with which he appeared satisfied having been given, the matter dropped.—The meeting terminated shortly after ten u'cleck, having lasted four hours.

div.head: FRODSEIAM FLOWER SHOW.
div.p: FRODSEIAM FLOWER SHOW.

The second annual show of the Frodsnam Floral zed Horticultural Society was held on Monday in a marquee erected in a field near the Parish Church, and was a grati- fying success. Last year when the first exhibition of the society took place the entries only numbered 284, this ycar they have risen to 617, an increase of 333. The Hon. Mrs ',oodles heads the list of patronesses, and the Rev. IL B. Blogg, vicar of the parish church, occupies the position of president, whilst there is an influential list of vice-presi- dents. Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., and Mr. R. Andrews cour- teously discharged the duties of hon. secretaries. Although 'dark clouds hung overhead and a cold wind blew from the west, the weather continued tine, and the attendance at the show was very encouraging. The local gentry appeared in strong force, and the visitors from the surrounding country and Rupacorn were very numerous. Selections of music by the Chester band of the 2nd C.R.1.7 lent additional attrac- tion to the affair. It should he mentioned that a stall con- taining a variety of fancy articles was presided over by Mrs John Ashton, Mrs C. A. Linaker, and the Misses Cros- field, the proceeds to be devoted to the restoration fund of the parish church. The judges were as follows :—Plants and flowers, Mr. Joseph Norval, Newton Nurseries; Mr. George Usher, Newton Nurseries; celery, Dr. Robinson and Mr. J. Pollard, Frodsham ; driftage gardens. Mr. R. Holland, Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., and Mr. R. Andrews, Frod- sham ; cheese, butter, fowls, and eggs, Mr. H. Linaker, Fro d- sham, and Mr. Thompson, Liverpotl. . .

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
THIIIISDAY—Bofore his Honour Judge Ffoulkes.

BANKRUPTCY.—The public examination -of James Towns- end Moore, solicitor, Cloth Hall-yard, was fixed for this sitting. Mr. Ridgway, official receiver, was present, and Mr. Riley, who appeared on behalf of the bankrupt, applied for an adjlurnment until next court day.—The application was granted.—An application was made to adjudicate Mr. William Porter, builder, a bankrupt, by Mr. Davies, on be- half of the executors of the late Mr. Porter. Mr. Wellhead, on behalf of Mr. Porter, consented, and an order was made. A CONTRACTOR'S CLAlM—Joseph Pennington v. James Stewart. —This was a claim for damages for bad work at a sewer at Wargrave-road, Earleetown, and for loss sustained from interference with gas mains. Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, for the defendant. The claim arose in reference to a contract for work entered into by the parties, and the plaintiff's case was that through the earth not being " punned" properly in filling up a sewer, it had since sunk, and had to be refinished, the cost of which was now sought from defendant. The rest of the claim was for loss of gas and cost of repairing gas pipes, rendered necessary by the sides of the sewer falling in, owing to their not having been properly " shorat "up. The case occupied the Court the whole of the afternoon, and when his Honour rose the plaintiff's solicitor had yet to reply. The case was the,efore adjourned until next Court when the reply will be made and judgment given. An ap- plication by Mr. Riley for payment out of Court of £lO. recovered by Stewart in a former action (as previously re- ported) was not acceeded to.

THE' SERVING OF SUMMONSES.—A woman appeared in answer to two summonses, which, she said, bad been left at her house by a bailiff, after he had been informed that the par- ties for whom they were intended did not reside there. She refused to accept the summonses, and the bailiff took them away, but last week someone left them with her son, before she was up. The parties bad not lived at her house for some monae.—The bailiff, questioned by his Honour, said that when he served the summonses on the boy the wom4n was there, and he asked her if she was the wife of one of the defendant&—His Honour commented on the con- duct of the bailiff, who, according to his own showing, had made returns that were false, because the endorsement said one summons was served upon a female, and the other upon the wife of the defendant.

NEWTON VOLITNTEEES AT A LDEESTIOT. —Oil Saturday morning about 50 men of the Newton Company of the 10th L.R.V. (Liverpool Press Guards) will leave Etrlestown station to undergo a ‘veA's training at the gre it military centre, Aldershot. The men will Muster at Newton about half-past six in the morning, and march along Crow-lane to Esrlestown station, where about 7-30 they will start for Crewe, and from thence to their destination. UNJUST SCALES AT WHISTON —At the Preseot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. W. L. Evans and H. D. Willis, Richard Prescott, a coal dealer, at Whistpn, pleaded guilty to having a p tir of unjust scales in his nos- Session. Superintendent Barker Stated that he visited the defendant's premises, and found the scales unjust. At the weight end was a piece of loose iron, weighing about Sibs., while in addition to that the scales were about 4-11). out of balance against the purchaser. The defendant was fined 103 and costs.
I WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse on Friday morning. There were present Mr C Broadbent (chairman), the Rev (3- F Roberts, and Messrs Z Aimitage, Jolley, Brown, J Houghton, W Houghton, KU- shall, Derbyshire; S Sutton (clerk), J C Sutton (assistant clerk), Dr tsephton (medical officer), W Owen (surveyor), and G Rawlings (inspector).

PENILETIC PAROCHI&L COMMITTEE. The minutes of a meeting of this committee, held on the 13th July, at which there were present Messrs J C Rmt- ledge (chairman), Forster, Hughes, and Grange Dr Seph- ton (medical officer), W Owen (surveyor), G Rawlings (inspector), and 8 Sutton (clerk), were read, ant stated that after a discussion on the subject of the Local Government Board's letter referring to the sewage of the district, it was agreed to authorise the chairman tl prepare another set of 1 plans providing for filtration of the sewage through tank and land before entering the brook. It was also agreed that the chairman should be empowered to purchase creosoted tacks for the purpose.—Mr OWEN said plans bad been pre- pared by Mr Routledge, which he was afraid would not be approved by the Local Government Beard.—lr was resolved that the plans should he referred back to the chairman of the Authority and Mr Owen. and they were empowered to forward them to the Local Government Board on their be- ing amended.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AND TEE SEWERAGE.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AND TEE SEWERAGE.

Some discussion took place as to the delay caused in the carrying out of sewerage works by the proposed Ship Canal.—The CHAIRMAN said it might be three or four years yet before the works in connection with the canal were car- ried out, and in the meanwhile the people living in certain parts of their district might suffer for want of proper drain- age. If they undertook the work in the meantime, would they be re-imbursed by the Ship Canal promoters ?—Mr OWEN was afield the cost of those works would fall upon the Authority, but he did not think it was likely there would be any need for anything of that kind. The canal would be a great advantage to their drainage after it was made.

div.head: – MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: - MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. SEPIITON reported that for the month ending July 31st the births were, males 21, females 15; deaths, males 8, females 7. The excess of births over deaths was 21, and the death rate from all causes was equal to 138 per 1000; against 11.4 in the corresponding period of last year. Re- ferring to precautions to be used against cholera, he sug- gested that the inspector be requested to make a house to house visitation of the most populous part of the Authority's district and ascertain that the drainage was good, the gullies cleaned out, the house drained well and efficiently trapped, the cesspools frequently emptied, the water supply good and efficient, and that no heaps of decaying vegetables or animal filth be allowed to accumulate, and report any insanitary conditiou or defect met with in his visitation to the Au- thority.—This report was confirmed..

div.head: SITRVEYOR El REPORT.
div.p: SITRVEYOR El REPORT.

Mr. CWEN, surveyor, reported that during the month inspections had been made of the following buildings:— Mr. Teflon's and Mr. Hindley'a houses, Padgate ; Mr. Mil- lington's honsm, Peaketh ; Mr. W. Bennett's cottages, Pad- gate; Penketh school; Mr. J. L'oyd's houses, Welfield- street, Warrington; Mr. Bostock's houses, 'Liverpool-road, Warrington; and Mr. Dornvllle's farm at flurtonwood. The following plans were submitted, and as they were in ac- cordance with the bye-laws they might be adopted :—Mr. Hawkins, feur houses at Padgate ; Sankey School Board, schoolmaster's house, Great Sankey; Mr. G. Grange, house, Great Sankey; Friends' school, additions, Penketh ; Mr. W. Bennett, addition to cottages, Padgate ; Mr. T. Alty, new pail c'osets, Rixten ; Mr. Hunt, farm buildings, Penketh; Mr. John Lloyd, eight houses, Welfield-street, Sankey; Orford schools, conversion of t loset for pail and new wash- house, Orford. He had issued the certificate of habitation to Mr. Milling'on for houses at Penketh. The Penketh Tannery Company had written that they were about to erect a new drying shed, but that the plans were not yet completed for submission. On the 13th July he attended the meeting of the Penketh Parochial Committee, 89 desired by the Authority. At the meeting it wis resolved that drawings should be prepared showing three settling pits, and also land sufficient for irrigation and filtration of sewerage between the tanks and the brook.—The report was adopted.

div.head: POLLUTION OF MORRIS BROOK.
div.p: POLLUTION OF MORRIS BROOK.

Mr. DAIIBYSHIRE Called attention to the pollution of Morris Brook, and said he thought the people who polluted the brook did not use all the means which were in their power to prevent that pollution.—lt was agreed that the inspector should be instructed to make an examination of the stream, and ascertain if all reasonable means were being adopted to prevent pollution. This was all the business.

PIES COT. BANK HOLIDAY AT PRESCOT.—On Monday there was nothing of a marked character in the town; the townspeople making their way to Huyton Sr St. Helens to enjoy the special attractions there provided. The shops and work- shops were all, with very few exceptions, closed all day on Monday aid Tuesday, and on the afternoon of Thursday as usual.

TRANSFERS.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, the following licenses were transferred :—Black Horse. F.troworth, to Frederick Simcock •, George Inn, Widnes to Selena Moore; Albion Hotel, Widnes, to John Burrow; Waterloo Vaults, Widnes, to Albert Hollingsworth ; beer- house in Victoria-street, Widnes, to William Abbott ; beer- house in Lugsdale-road, Widnes' to Joseph Ball. A DESTRUCTIVE Som.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Keenan, a young man, was charged under a warrant with wilfully breaking household furniture and other articles to the amount of £B, the property of his father, James Keenan. a labourer, residing at 88, Alfred- street, Wavertree, Liverpool. On the Bth July, during the absence of bis father, the prisoner visited his house, and because his mother ordered him to leave he seized a brush and smashed a large glass case containing china cups and saucers, glass ornaments, clic., and then smashed all the windows of the house. He was cammitted for trial at the next Quarter Sessions.

CONSERVATIVE CLUB Excunsiox.—The Working-men's Society having now bncome defunct, the annual excursion which used to take place under their auspices Lae now been taken up by the Conservative Club, but in order not to make it a one.sided affiir in a strictly political sense, it was planned to devote any oyerplus of funds realised to the Prescot Parish Nurse Fund ; consequently it was taken up by all parties with spirit, and on the morning of Tuesday over 700 wended their way to the station, and a train of twenty carriages left for Blackpool at ten minutes to seven, arriving there a little before ten. The party visited the very numerous places of interest and enjoyment, and made most of the day. The start back was at eight o'clock. POLICE ASSAULT AT KNOW6LEY.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, William Adams, a young man, lodg- ing in Present, WAS summoned for being drunk and dis- orderly in Knowlby-lane, on the 25th ult., also with assaulting P.C. Jackson and damaging his trousers to the value of is—P.C. Jackson deposed that at an early hour on the morning of the date named he found the defendant drunk and asleep on the footpath. He awoke the defendant, who said he came from Prescot, and they went along in that direction. The defendant then became very violent and struck him several times on the bee and body, threw him down and tore his trousers.—The defendant, who said the constable first abused him, was fined ss. and costa for the drunkenness, 20s. and costs for the assault, and he was ordered to pay is. as damage to the trousers. SERIOUS DISTURBANCE AT PRESCOT.--.I3efOTS Mr. W. L. Evans and Captain Willis, at the Present Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, two young women named Mary eilgannon and Sarah Mannien were summoned for assaulting Mary Ellen • Murray, a young woman, in Hill-street, Prescot. on the 23rd July.—The complainant stated that the defendaat 1 Gilgannon seized her by the hair of her heed. and dragged I her along the street, while the defendant 31annion lucked her on the legs. aud struck her on tle head with a large stone, which cat her head. She had the wound dressed by Dr. Green.—Superintendent Barker remarked that the I neighbourhood in question was in a continual state of dis- turbance—P.S. Bull said that the complainant came to the I olice office and charged the defendants with haying as- saulted her. She was then bleeding from a wound on the head, which seemed to be cut to the bone.—The defendants accused the complainant and her friends of having thrown stones, and said they Only acted in defence.—The two de- fendants had previously been convicted for disorderly con- duct, and they were each fined 103 and costs.

div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.

On Friday, Lord Carnarvon conferred thejihonour of Knighthood on the Mayor of Derry. _ It is stated as probable that the Duke of Connaught will succeed Sir Thomas Steele as Com.nander-in-Chief in Ireland.
A mass of chalk on Friday morning fell on two men working in a chalk pit at Dover. One of them was danger- ously injured.
LOrd (;arnarvon will leave the Viceregal Lodge, Dublin, on Monday next, for the ten days' tour in the South and West of Ireland.

'homas Hairsine, late secretary of the Sunderland Co- operative Society, was on Friday committed for trial on several charges of embezzlement. Sir H. D. Wolff had an interview with the Marquis of Salisbury at Arlington-street on Friday morning, prepara- tory to his departure for the East. On Thursday a thunderstorm broke over Accrington and diszrict. A valuable horse belonging to Mr. John Sud- eten. farmer, Huncoat, was struck with the electric fluid and killed.

TWO MEN KILLED.—TWO foremen surfacemen—Charles M`Quigan, of Paisley, and Allan Cameron, of Elderslie— were knocked down and killed at Elderelie Station on Friday morning by a Large express. I'RE DENARY RIOTS.—At Leeds Assizes, on Friday, 15 colliers were indicted for rioting at Denaby Main Collieries during the recent strike. Five were sentenced to four menthe' imprisonment each, and the rest were released on their re- cognisances.

THE Inisit LIBEL Casu —The Irish Appeal Court on Fri- day upheld the decision of the Queen's Bench Division, which refused the defendant a new trial in the libel action Bolton versus O'Brien, editor of " United Ireland," in which the plaintiff was awarded three thousand pounds damages.

FIGHTING AMONGST MILITIAMEN.—A serious fracas took place amongst the Royal Irish Militia, at Dover, on Friday tnbrning. Three privates, who had evidently been drinking throughout the night, made a raid upon a number of licen- sed victuallers who bad refused to supply them with liquor. In the Course of the mel(s3 the picquet had to draw their bayonets, and one of the men was seriously wounded in the forehead.

CLOSE OF THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.—The closing session of the Wesleyan Conference was held on Friday morning, the attendance being very much smaller than on the previous days. A variety of miscellaneous business relating to middle class education, notices of motion, and suggestions from districts, were rapidly disposed of. The reading of the journal and votes of thanks followed ; and, at noon, the fifth Newcastle conference and the one hundred and forty-second annual Wesleyan conference came to an end.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR CHESTER.—A rail way accident of a shocking character occurred near Chester on Friday morning to a little girl named Amy Sullivan, who resides at Salford. Whilst looking through the carriage window when the train was proceeding at a good pace the girl fell through the window and on to the permanent way. Infor- mation of the accident was conveyed to the railway offi- cials, and a light engine was immediately forwarded from Chester. She was found lying insensible on the line, and was taken to the Chester General Infirmary, where she now lies in a most precarious condition.

THE FRENCH ELECTIONS. A Central News telegram, dated Paris, Friday, says : At a Council of Ministers held here this morning the date of the forthcoining elections to the Legislature was fixed for the 4th of October.

RUSSIAN WARLIKE ACTIVITY. Sr. PETERSBURG, PRIDAY,—A resolution of the Council of War, sanctioned by the Emperor, directs the formation of a separate artillery department for the Transeasplan terri- tory. A considerable supply of newly-manufactured shells for the Siberian flotilla will shortly be despatched to Viabivostock.
A Central News telegram, dated S. Petersburg, Tlihrs- day night, says :—warlike feeling here daring the past two days has greatly increased.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

-- --- The House met at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Marquis of SALISBURY, replying to Lord Sandhurst, said the Government could give no guarantee with regard to the completion of the Varna and Rutschuck Railway.-1 he Parliamentary Elections (Re- turniag Officers) Bill was read a third time. The Labourers' (Ireland, No. 2) Bill passed through Committee.—After a long discussion, the Earl of IDDESLEIGII, in the absence of the Prime Minister, presented a hill relating to the public health of the metropolis, end it was read a first time. The House adjourned during pleasure. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at four o'cloCk.---- QUESTIONS.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, re- plying to Mr. Arnold, said Lord Iddesleigh would in a few days, make a statement in the House of Lords with regard to the Royal Commission on trade depression, after which he should be happy to give any further explanation that might be require J.—Mr. BOURKE, replying to Mr. Monk, said he was not then able to state the decision arrived at by the Conference at Paris relative to the Suez Canal, but papers would be laid on the table in a few days. THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT BILL—The House then proceeded to further consider the Criminal Law Amendment Bill.—Mr. C. BENTINCE proposed to add to clause 2, which dealt with procuration, the following words :—" That no person should be convicted of any offence under this section upon the evidence of one witness, unless such witness be corroborated in some material particular." Mr. Ben- tinck's proposal was agreed to. The proviso having been amended by adding to it the following words —" by evidence tending. to implicate the accused," was ordered to stand part of the Bill. Sir R. CROSS moved an addition to clause 3, which provided punishment for procuring by threats or fraud.—lt was agreed to after an amendment by Sir H. James, who also moved to amend the 4th clause relating to offences against children under 14, so as to enable the evidence of the girl to to be received though not given on oath.—Mr. WHITBREAD wished that the same rule should apply to other witnesses. —Sir R. CROSS accepted the amendment, which', after being further amended to provide that the evidence so ' given should be corroborated, was agreed to. Mr. BROADHURST moved a further addition to the clause —A long discussion ensued, Mr. BROADHURS I' defending his proposal by Insisting that a boy who never had moral training ought not to be punished in the same way as a bey who had been well brought up in a comfortable horne.—For the proviso, 20; against, 63.

GOLBORNE. TLLE NEW RECTOR.—The Rev. T. W. Richardson, the newly appointed Rector of Golborne, haa not entered uPee his duties, it being understood that he is away on his holii- d-qa. Meanwhile the curate, the Rev. W. Thcrp, has charge of the parish. CONSERVATIVE Pic-mc.—The fifth annual pic-nic under the auspices of the Ciolborne Workiugenen's Club was held on Wednesday. A goodly numl.er of members, together with their wives and frienda, assembled at the club at nine o'clock. Sale had been selected for the day's oure and the party were conveyed thither in waggonettes. The Botanical Gardens, for which Sale has become celebrated, proved an attractive source of enjoymeet, the whole of the time being profitably spent therein. In the evening a sub- stantial tea was provided for the party. The return jour- ney was commenced about seven o'clock, the deraece being Covered in a little over four hours. KILLED BY A RUNAWAY HORSE.—Mr, B. ighouse, tbn county coroner, held an inquest at the Angel Hotel, Edge Green, Gulborne, on Tuesday morning, touching the death of a Liverpool buy, five years of age, named Wilfred Haul Taylor, wnose death resulted from a shocking accident on the morning of Friday. The evidence brought out the foie lowing facts :—Deceaeed was the . an of Mr. Thomas Taylor, a clerk residing at No. 40. Rice-lane, Walren. He WaS grandson to Mr. John Parkinson, of Edge Green, Golborner with whom be was spending his holidays. On Friday fore: . noon dece..eed was noticed sitting on a rate post at the end of the lane in which his grandfather's house is situated. A horse and trap stood in the lane, the animal grazing while the man who was supposed to be in charge was delivering _- some flour at Mr. Cook's, next floor to Mr. Parkinson's- During his absence the head . halter C4OlO off, an i the hors took fright in the direction where deceased sar, and before , the poor boy could escape the trap dashed iuto him, one of the shafts entering his body, inflicting a wouucl from which I be died before a doctor could be called in. A post mortal he was ordered to be made by Dr. Hannah, a , Ashton, who stated death was attributable to internal rupture- -41. verdict of accidental death was returned, and the low man exprested on behalf of the jury, a hope that ilighaus would not leave his horse in future. He also stated that it 1. was a common practice to leave a horse by the roadside. 0 and they did not therefore wish to blame the Inen.—Tee Coroner, addressing Higham, said the jury had taken , moat lenient view of the cote and if they had teought hire . in culptbly negligent he would have hod no tesitation concurring with their verdict and cernmittitig him for man' slaughter.
